Controls are reviewed when the architecture changes, when a lower-level invariant replaces a higher-level instruction, when the protected failure has stayed away across the window, or when the control blocks legitimate work more than it prevents harm. Retirement needs evidence too.

### Metrics close the loop

The signals only mean something against metrics defined before the result: outcome, guardrail and counter-metric, each with a threshold, a window and a source. The ratchet then changes the outcome frame, the assumptions, the slice or the measurement plan for product evidence, and the tests, context, scope or handoff for coding-agent corrections. Incidents can change both.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Two teams share the assistant and disagree on a tradeoff a signal exposes. Where does it go? Expected: to a shaped backlog item with a human decision owner; the ratchet does not resolve product disagreements by itself.
- **Level 4:** How do you prioritize across many signals? Expected: by consequence and recurrence together, so a severe single event and a frequent minor one both rise above a rare minor one.
- **Level 4:** What proves the loop works after a quarter? Expected: named controls that trace back to signals, verification results that show recurrence fell, and retirements with their evidence; not the volume of telemetry collected.

## Wrong answers

- "Build a dashboard so everyone can see the signals." Visibility without promotion and ownership changes nothing.
- "Add each lesson learned to the system prompt." Prose is the weakest layer; a permission boundary can make the unsafe action impossible, and a test can block a release that repeats the failure.
- "Keep every control forever since it was earned." Controls decay and conflict; each one needs a retirement condition and periodic review.

## Taught in

The [feedback ratchet lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/54-build-the-feedback-ratchet/) gives the routing table and the ownership fields, and the [success metrics lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/52-design-success-metrics/) gives the metric contract the signals are judged against.

interviews.title: Leave work so that someone else can resume it
interviews.markdown:
Your session ends without warning in the middle of a multi-step change, and a colleague picks it up the next morning. What must they be able to find, and where?

## Short answer

They need to see which items are done, which proof ran for each one, which files changed, which dependencies are now unblocked, and what the next safe item is. That state lives next to the work, in the repository, as small items with explicit proof, not as checked boxes inside a chat.

## Full answer

### Design for interruption

Sessions end unexpectedly. A resumable plan has work items small enough that another person, or another agent, can determine the state of each one from the artifacts alone. The five things they must be able to read:

- which item is complete;
- which proof ran and what it returned;
- which artifacts changed;
- which dependencies are now unblocked;
- what the next safe item is.

### Why chat is the wrong place

A checked box in a conversation says that someone believed an item was done. It does not say which command proved it or which files it touched. The next person either trusts the box or redoes the work. A plan stored next to the code, with one identifier per item and the proof command written down, lets them verify instead of trust.

### The habit

I stop at item boundaries when I can. When I cannot, the plan still shows the last proof that passed, so the resume point is the first item whose proof has not run.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 1:** Where do you keep the plan? Expected: in the repository next to the work, as the source of truth, with any rendering such as a Markdown view generated from it.
- **Level 2:** An item is marked done but has no proof recorded. What does the colleague do? Expected: treat it as not done and run its proof; a box without proof is a belief.
- **Level 2:** Why does item size matter for resumption? Expected: a small item either finished or did not; a large half-done item forces the next person to reconstruct where it stopped.

## Wrong answers

- "Write a summary message at the end of the session." The session can end before the summary; the state must exist as the work proceeds.
- "The git log is enough." Commits show what changed, not which proof ran or which item is next.
- "Only the person who started can finish it." That is the failure the plan should prevent.

## Taught in

The [evidence-backed plan lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/44-plan-from-evidence/) covers designing a plan for interruption and storing it next to the work.

interviews.title: Write a specification that leaves judgment where it belongs
interviews.markdown:
You hand a task to a coding agent, or to a new engineer, to add a read-only diagnosis step to an incident tool. Last time the brief was two sentences and the result guessed the system. The time before, the brief was a twelve-page design and the result transcribed a mistake in it. How do you write this one?

## Short answer

I write an executable contract with six surfaces: the outcome, the invariants that must always hold, concrete examples, non-goals, a decision policy, and the proof required before completion. Every decision is marked locked, bounded or delegated by its consequence and reversibility. The production-write boundary is locked, the time budget for the data source is bounded, and local structure and names are delegated with an explanation required.

## Full answer

### Two bad extremes

An underspecified task makes the builder guess the system. An overspecified task makes the builder transcribe a design that may already be wrong. The useful middle fixes invariants and evidence and leaves reversible choices open.

### The six surfaces

| Surface | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Outcome | The observable result |
| Invariants | Conditions that must always stay true |
| Examples | Concrete cases that show intent |
| Non-goals | Adjacent behavior excluded on purpose |
| Decision policy | Which choices are locked, bounded or delegated |
| Proof | Evidence required before completion |

### Three decision modes

- Locked: the builder must not choose. Public compatibility, authority, safety, irreversible cost, product commitments.
- Bounded: the builder may choose inside explicit limits. Search budgets, retry counts, allowed dependencies, a known interface family.
- Delegated: the builder owns the choice and explains it. Local structure, names, reversible refactors, implementation detail.

"The implementation may use any read-only source that returns inside the time budget" is not vague. It is a delegated decision with a boundary and a proof.

### Examples compress intent

"Helpful", "robust" and "production-ready" are not executable. A small set of normal, edge, failure and forbidden cases gives the builder and the verifier the same target. Examples do not replace invariants; one passing case cannot prove a universal safety rule.

### Proof matches the claim

A unit test proves a local function contract. A wire test proves serialization and transport. A browser journey proves an interface path. A replay set proves behavior over representative cases. An audit log proves that authority boundaries held. I do not accept a lower layer as proof of a higher-layer claim.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Someone moves the production-write decision from locked to delegated. The schema accepts it. Why is it still wrong? Expected: the schema checks shape, not product risk; a write to production is irreversible and changes authority, so it stays locked.
- **Level 3:** A retry count is set to a fixed number in the brief. Is that locked or bounded? Expected: bounded is the better mode; the builder may pick inside a stated range and the range carries the reason.
- **Level 4:** Three implementation instructions describe the same behavior. What do you replace them with? Expected: one invariant and two examples, so the intent survives a change of implementation.
- **Level 4:** Why record the reason behind each locked choice? Expected: so a later team can revise it when the evidence changes, without archaeology through old threads.

## Wrong answers

- "Specify every step so nothing can go wrong." A step-by-step script transcribes the author's mistakes and removes the judgment that catches them.
- "Give the goal and trust the builder." Without invariants and proof, the builder guesses the system and the result cannot be verified.
- "A passing unit test proves the feature works." A unit test proves a local contract, not an interface path or an authority boundary.

## Taught in

The [specification lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/51-write-specifications-that-preserve-judgment/) gives the six surfaces, the three decision modes and the rule that proof must match the claim.

interviews.title: Set the success metric before the first result exists
interviews.markdown:
Tell me about a time you defined how a project would be judged before you had any results. What did you write down, and what did you refuse to leave open until later?

## Short answer

I start from the goal, derive the questions it raises, and only then pick the smallest metrics that answer them. Each metric gets a direction, a threshold, a window, a source and a population before any value is observed, and each outcome metric is paired with a guardrail and a counter-metric. I also write the pass, fail and ambiguous decisions in advance, because a team that sees the result first moves the threshold to protect the build.

## Full answer

### Goal, question, metric

For an incident tool the goal was to cut the time to identify the affected service without raising unsafe actions. The questions followed: how fast is the correct service found, how often is it correct, does diagnosis stay read-only, and does the workflow raise alert dismissal or operator load. The metrics made each question operational.

### A metric needs a contract

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Name | median identification seconds |
| Direction | at most |
| Threshold | 120 |
| Window | ten incident replays |
| Source | the replay event log |
| Population | the on-call engineers in the pilot |
| Kind | outcome or guardrail |

Without a source and a window a number cannot be reproduced. Without a threshold it cannot drive a decision.

### Three kinds of metric

- Outcome: did the desired state improve?
- Guardrail: did a fixed constraint stay true?
- Counter-metric: did the local gain shift cost or harm somewhere else?

Speed alone is not enough. Correctness, production writes, operator workload and missed alerts protect against a fast but unsafe result. A plan without a guardrail is invalid even when the outcome metrics look complete.

### Decide before you measure

The lesson's example: pass when the correct-service rate is at least 0.9 and the median time is at most 120 seconds; fail on any production write or a correct rate below 0.75; ambiguous when the gain is small with wide variance, which calls for a larger replay set. A stable correct rate between 0.75 and 0.9 matches none of the three rules, so I also write a rule for it before the replay: it does not pass, and it names the next test. Offline replay gives repeatability and edge coverage. A bounded pilot gives real behavior and trust. I use the cheapest evidence that answers the current decision and do not expose real users only because the code is ready.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** A metric is easy to collect but cannot change the decision. What do you do with it? Expected: remove it; measurement answers a decision, it does not decorate a dashboard.
- **Level 2:** Give a counter-metric for the incident tool. Expected: review time added for the incident commander, or escalations that moved to another team.
- **Level 3:** The outcome metric passes and the guardrail fails. What is the verdict? Expected: fail; a fixed constraint that broke means the outcome was not reached.
- **Level 3:** Results come back ambiguous. What was already written for that case? Expected: the next step, such as a larger replay set, decided before the result so nobody argues the threshold afterwards.

## Wrong answers

- "Pick the metric after you see what the system can do." The threshold then moves to protect the build and the measurement decides nothing.
- "One good outcome metric is enough." Without a guardrail, a fast but unsafe result passes.
- "Run a live pilot since the implementation is ready." Readiness is not a reason to expose users; the cheapest evidence that answers the decision comes first.

## Taught in

The [success metrics lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/52-design-success-metrics/) gives the metric contract, the three kinds of metric and the rule to decide before measuring.

interviews.title: Reframe a request that names its own solution
interviews.markdown:
A product manager asks you to build an incident assistant for the on-call team. You have one week. Before you plan any work, what do you ask, and what do you write down first?

## Short answer

The request names an artifact, not a result. I write an outcome frame first: who has the problem, when it happens, what they do today, which observable state must improve, which limits are fixed, and which nearby work is out of scope. Then I check the frame for a product form, a model or an architecture that no evidence supports yet.

## Full answer

### The six parts of the frame

| Part | Question I answer |
|---|---|
| User | Who feels the problem directly? |
| Situation | When and where does it happen? |
| Current behavior | What happens today, including the workarounds? |
| Desired outcome | Which observable state must get better? |
| Constraints | Which safety, policy, cost or compatibility limits are fixed? |
| Non-goals | Which tempting adjacent work is excluded? |

For the on-call team, the desired outcome could read: when an alert arrives, the engineer finds the failing service and one safe next step inside the incident time budget, and the diagnosis stays read-only and auditable. A runbook, a data repair or a smaller interface change can all satisfy that sentence. The team stays attached to the result, not to the first tool someone imagined.

### Leakage

A frame leaks a solution when it contains an interface, a model choice, a framework or a storage system that evidence has not earned. "Users get a weekly summary from a model" leaks the summary and the cadence. "Users understand account changes before approval" states the result. A constraint can name a technology when compatibility really fixes it. I record why it is fixed.

### Constraints and non-goals do real work

Constraints are part of the goal. No production writes during diagnosis, a response inside the incident time budget, and no new runtime dependency all remove whole classes of solutions. Non-goals keep the first slice from growing into a platform: no automatic remediation, no new alert routing, no replacement of the incident commander.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 1:** How do you tell an outcome from an output? Expected: an outcome names an observable change for a user; an output names an artifact such as a page, a tool or a model.
- **Level 2:** The manager insists on a chat interface. Where does that go in the frame? Expected: into the constraints only when policy or compatibility fixes it, with the reason written down; otherwise it waits for evidence.
- **Level 2:** Name two non-goals that keep the first slice small. Expected: no automatic fix of the incident and no new alert routing, for example; each one must be concrete enough to reject work.
- **Level 3:** What is the first observation that would show the desired outcome is wrong? Expected: a measured time to find the failing service that is already short, which means the frame targets a problem that does not exist.

## Wrong answers

- "Start with the interface and refine the goal later." The interface is one output. It ties the team to the first artifact before anyone knows what must improve.
- "Constraints are implementation details for later." A build that reaches the outcome and breaks a constraint has not reached the outcome.
- "Non-goals are optional." Without them, a useful slice grows into a platform before the first result is measured.

## Taught in

The [outcome frame lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/47-outcomes-before-output/) gives the six-part frame and the leakage check.

interviews.title: What you check before you approve an execution plan
interviews.markdown:
A teammate, or a coding agent, hands you this plan for a change to a public API: update the endpoint, add tests, update the documentation. They want approval to start. What do you ask for before you say yes, and what would make you reject the plan outright?

## Short answer

That list repeats the request in future tense. I ask for five things on each item: a stable identifier, the smallest change, the repository facts that justify it, the items it depends on, and the exact check that closes it. I reject a plan with a duplicate identifier, an item without evidence or proof, a dependency on an unknown item, a cycle, or an irreversible step scheduled before the uncertainty it depends on is resolved.

## Full answer

### Why the three-line plan fails

Nothing in it says what was found in the repository, why those files are the right ones, which contract changes first, or what can run at the same time. Someone can complete every line and still create rework.

### The five commitments

| Commitment | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Identifier | A stable reference for dependencies and handoff |
| Change | The smallest behavior or contract change |
| Evidence | Repository facts that justify the change |
| Dependencies | Work that must be true first |
| Proof | The exact check that closes the item |

### Order by dependency, not by prose

When several surfaces depend on one behavior, the contract comes first. Tests, implementation and documentation then share one definition instead of inventing four. A dependency graph also shows safe concurrency: implementation and documentation can proceed together after the contract is fixed, and the integration gate waits for both.

### Evidence must be able to change the plan

An existing helper removes a planned abstraction. A compatibility test forces a migration step. A deployment constraint moves a schema change into another task. If a piece of evidence cannot change the plan, it is decoration, not evidence.

### The rejection list

The first five checks are mechanical: duplicate identifiers, items without evidence, items without proof, unknown dependencies, cycles. The last check needs judgment: does the first irreversible action, such as a migration or a public release, happen before the relevant uncertainty is resolved? I call that one out explicitly in the review.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** One item lists two proof commands. What do you do? Expected: split it into two items, because one item needs one clear completion proof.
- **Level 2:** Two items depend on each other. What does that usually hide? Expected: an unresolved product or design disagreement; the cycle is the symptom, the missing decision is the cause.
- **Level 3:** The plan sits in a chat thread as checked boxes. Why is that a problem? Expected: a session can end at any moment, and another person cannot see which proof ran or which item is now unblocked; the plan belongs next to the work.
- **Level 3:** A migration item needs a human approval. How do you express that in the graph? Expected: as an explicit item with the approval as its proof, which every dependent item waits for.

## Wrong answers

- "Trust the author and review the result instead." Rework found at review time costs more than a plan rejected before editing.
- "A longer plan is a better plan." Length adds nothing; evidence and proof on each item do.
- "Dependencies are obvious from the order of the list." Prose order hides which steps can run together and which must wait.

## Taught in

The [evidence-backed plan lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/44-plan-from-evidence/) gives the five commitments and the validation rules.

interviews.title: A prototype that quietly acquired real users
interviews.markdown:
You discover that a weekend prototype you shared internally is now used every day by another team, with production data, and someone just reported an outage to you. Walk me through what went wrong before this moment and what you do in the first week.

## Short answer

The system drifted across stages. It gained users, data and authority without gaining ownership, and nothing in the system itself marked it as a prototype. In the first week I make the stage observable in configuration, access control, telemetry and documentation, cut the production data path until a named owner accepts it, and decide with that team whether the right next stage is a bounded pilot or a stop.

## Full answer

### Three stages ask three questions

| Stage | Primary question |
|---|---|
| Prototype | Can this mechanism produce the evidence at all? |
| Pilot | Does it work safely with a bounded real audience and real conditions? |
| Production | Can we own it continuously at the promised reliability and risk level? |

These are learning environments, not levels of polish. A prototype can be technically complete and still be disposable. Production begins when the organization accepts ongoing responsibility.

### What went wrong

The prototype was built for one question and had no false operational guarantees, which was right. The failure was stage drift: it acquired an audience, real data and the authority to affect another team's work, and nobody acquired ownership. A warning banner would not have prevented this. The stage has to be enforced by the system: a configuration flag that blocks production data, access control that limits the audience, telemetry that shows who uses it, and documentation that says what it is.

### The first week

1. Stop the bleeding: block the production data path with a technical control, not a message.
2. Name the stage in the system so anyone can see it.
3. Meet the other team with the pilot requirements: a named audience, a human owner, bounded duration and authority, audit and rollback, outcome and guardrail thresholds, and exit criteria for expand, revise or stop.
4. Decide. If no one will own it, the honest outcome is a stop, and the evidence it produced still counts.

### What production would require

A service level objective, on-call and incident ownership, security and privacy review, cost and capacity controls, rollback and recovery, continuous monitoring, and a retirement path. Deployment is not production. Ownership is.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** The other team says the outage shows the tool is valuable. How do you answer? Expected: value is a reason to run a bounded pilot with an owner, not a reason to keep an unowned system on production data.
- **Level 3:** Which technical control would have prevented the drift? Expected: a configuration or access control that refuses production data unless the stage is set to pilot or production by an owner.
- **Level 4:** What is the first operational responsibility that makes a build production? Expected: someone accepts an on-call or incident ownership commitment; before that, the system has users but no owner.
- **Level 4:** The team wants to skip the pilot and go straight to production. What evidence would justify that? Expected: low consequence, operational readiness, and measured outcome and guardrail results from a bounded real audience.

## Wrong answers

- "Add a banner that says prototype." A banner does not stop data, users or authority from flowing in.
- "Harden the prototype into the product since people already use it." Prototype code earned another stage only if the evidence says so; usage is not that evidence.
- "Shut it down with no discussion." The evidence it produced is real; the decision owner needs options, not a surprise.

## Taught in

The [prototype, pilot or production lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/53-prototype-pilot-or-production/) gives the three stage questions, the pilot requirements and the stage drift controls.

interviews.title: Decide what to delete from a bloated instruction file
interviews.markdown:
A team's agent instruction file has grown for a year. Rules contradict each other, the context is heavy, and nobody remembers why half of them exist. You are asked to clean it up. How do you decide what stays, what goes, and what you will not touch yet?

## Short answer

Every control needs a retirement condition, and retirement needs evidence like any other change. I review each rule against four questions: did the architecture or workflow it protected change, did a stronger executable control replace it, has the failure stayed away across a meaningful window, and does the rule block legitimate work more often than it prevents harm. A rule that passes none of those stays, and a rule I cannot trace to a cause gets an owner and a review date before it gets deleted.

## Full answer

### Why the file grew

Each rule was a correction promoted into prose. Prose is the weakest durable layer. Over a year the rules encoded a system that no longer exists, started to conflict, and now consume context on every run. The goal is not the longest instruction file. It is the smallest system that preserves hard-won judgment.

### The review

| Question | If yes |
|---|---|
| Did the architecture or workflow change? | The rule protects a system that is gone; retire it |
| Did a type, a test or a permission replace it? | Delete the prose and keep the executable control |
| Has the failure not recurred across the window? | Retire it, and note the window as the evidence |
| Does it block legitimate work more than it prevents harm? | Rewrite it narrower or retire it |

### Replace before delete

For a rule that still protects a real risk, the better move is often promotion rather than retirement: a prose rule about output shape becomes an example plus a validator, a prose rule about files becomes a scope policy. I delete the sentence only after proving the stronger control exists and fires.

### What I do not touch yet

A rule with no recorded cause and no owner is a gap in the record, not a candidate for deletion. I give it an owner and a review date, and I look for the correction that created it. Deleting it because it feels old is the mistake the lesson warns against.

### Guard against regrowth

Every new control gets an owner, a verification, a review or expiry window and a retirement condition when it is created. Without that, the file fills again in a year.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Two rules contradict each other. What do you do first? Expected: find the cause behind each; a contradiction usually means one of them protects a system or decision that changed.
- **Level 3:** A rule has not fired in months. Is that enough to delete it? Expected: only if the window is meaningful for that failure and the risk it protected is still visible elsewhere; low frequency with high consequence can keep a rule alive.
- **Level 4:** How do you show that a deletion was safe? Expected: the stronger control that replaced it fires on the original failure case, and the recurrence stays absent across the review window.
- **Level 4:** What stops the file from growing back? Expected: a creation rule that every control carries an owner, a verification and a retirement condition, with periodic review.

## Wrong answers

- "Delete everything older than a year and see what breaks." Retirement needs evidence; a silent failure can take months to appear.
- "Keep all of it, context is cheap." Stale rules conflict, encode a dead system and bloat every run.
- "Rewrite the whole file from scratch." The file holds judgment that was paid for; the job is to move it to stronger layers, not to lose it.

## Taught in

The [feedback-to-system lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/46-turn-feedback-into-system/) gives the retirement checks and the [feedback ratchet lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/54-build-the-feedback-ratchet/) gives the ownership and expiry fields.

interviews.title: Pick the first experiment from a roadmap of features
interviews.markdown:
You join a team with a quarter-long roadmap for an assistant that recommends a next action to on-call engineers. The roadmap lists features in priority order. Tell me how you decide what to work on in week one, and why it may not be the first roadmap item.

## Short answer

A roadmap hides uncertainty inside features. I rewrite the features as falsifiable assumptions about value, usability, feasibility, viability and safety, then score each one on impact, uncertainty and irreversibility. Week one goes to the cheapest decisive test of the highest open risk, which is often not the top roadmap item.

## Full answer

### Features are bets

The assistant only pays off if several conditions hold: alert context contains enough information to name a service, engineers trust a recommendation they did not derive, the response time matters operationally, the data is reachable without unsafe authority, and the workflow happens often enough to justify maintenance. None of these is an implementation task. They are conditions for the build to be worth doing.

### Five classes

| Class | Question |
|---|---|
| Value | Will the outcome matter enough? |
| Usability | Can the user understand and act on it? |
| Feasibility | Can the system produce it with the available data and limits? |
| Viability | Can the organization sustain the cost, the ownership and the operation? |
| Safety | Can it fail without an unacceptable consequence? |

An assumption has to be written so that it can be false. "The feature is useful" cannot be tested. "Eight of ten on-call engineers name the correct service faster with the read-only result" can.

### Risk is three numbers, not one

The lesson scores impact, uncertainty and irreversibility separately, each from one to five, multiplies impact by uncertainty and adds irreversibility. The formula is not sacred. Its job is to force the team to say why one unknown must be resolved before another. Irreversible, high-consequence choices need earlier evidence: a read-only replay can precede a production integration, and a human-approved recommendation can precede automatic action.

### An experiment, not a confirmation ritual

A useful test has a claim that could be false, a realistic sample, an observable result, a threshold decided before the result, and a next decision for pass, fail and ambiguous evidence. A demo that only shows the team can build the idea is not a test.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** The highest-risk assumption is tested and holds. What changes? Expected: it moves from open to tested with its evidence attached, and the next experiment targets the next highest open risk.
- **Level 2:** Which assumption class do feature lists most often omit? Expected: safety, the question of whether the feature can fail without unacceptable consequence.
- **Level 3:** The roadmap owner says the ranking already reflects risk. How do you check? Expected: compare the risk ranking with the roadmap order and explain each mismatch; where they differ, one of them is wrong about the evidence.
- **Level 3:** Write a threshold that would stop the build. Expected: for example, fewer than a stated share of engineers in the replay trust the read-only recommendation enough to act on it.

## Wrong answers

- "Build the first roadmap item; the order was agreed." Agreement on order is not evidence that the riskiest assumption holds.
- "Ship something small and see what happens." A small build without a claim, a threshold and a next decision learns nothing.
- "Risk is just how likely it is to fail." Impact and irreversibility change the order even when the probability is the same.

## Taught in

The [assumption map lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/49-map-assumptions-and-risk/) gives the five classes, the three risk dimensions and the shape of a decisive experiment.

interviews.title: Define the first slice so it can change the decision
interviews.markdown:
Your team agrees to ship a minimum viable version of a new assistant. Three proposals are on the table: a polished interface on synthetic data, a working data pipeline with no interface, and a read-only replay over ten real incidents. Which one do you argue for, and how do you justify the choice?

## Short answer

I argue for the replay over real incidents. Small is useful only when the slice proves something that matters, so I first write the required proof set from the highest-risk open assumptions and reject any candidate that does not cover it. The polished page over fake data and the pipeline without users each remove the exact uncertainty the team needs to test.

## Full answer

### Vertical means evidence end to end

A useful slice crosses the minimum real workflow needed to observe an outcome. It can be narrow in users, data, duration and capability. It must not be narrow by cutting out the uncertainty under test. The replay across ten real incidents tests service identification and operator trust at once. A polished page over fake data may test comprehension but not data feasibility. A production auto-remediator would test everything at once with unacceptable consequence.

### Required proof comes before scoring

I take the highest-risk open assumptions and turn them into a proof set. A candidate is eligible only if it covers that set. Among eligible candidates I compare outcome value, uncertainty reduced, effort, consequence and reversibility. The eligibility gate matters more than the arithmetic. A cheaper candidate that proves one required assumption stays ineligible even with a high score.

### False minimums I name in the room

- The interface-only minimum removes the data and operational uncertainty.
- The infrastructure-only minimum proves possibility without user value.
- The happy-path minimum omits the exception that creates most of the risk.
- The demo minimum produces a persuasive artifact but no repeatable measurement.
- The platform minimum builds reusable machinery before one workflow has earned it.

### The stop rule

Before anyone builds, I write what happens if the slice fails: abandon the outcome, change the target user, test a different mechanism, collect better evidence, or narrow authority further. If every possible result leads to "keep building", the slice is not an experiment.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** The replay fails. Name two valid next moves. Expected: change the target user or situation, or test a different mechanism; both were written in the stop rule before the build.
- **Level 2:** Why does a replay beat a live pilot here? Expected: it produces reversible evidence about trust and identification without exposing real users to a system nobody has measured.
- **Level 3:** A reusable component would speed up all three proposals. When does it get built? Expected: after the slice has produced decisive evidence; building platform machinery first is the platform minimum.
- **Level 3:** How do you keep the replay from becoming a demo? Expected: a repeatable measurement with a threshold decided in advance, not a persuasive walkthrough.

## Wrong answers

- "The smallest build is the one with the fewest features." Smallness is measured by the evidence gained, not by the feature count.
- "Build the interface first so stakeholders can see progress." A persuasive artifact without a measurement is the demo minimum.
- "If the slice fails we iterate." Without a written stop rule, every result leads to more building and nothing was tested.

## Taught in

The [smallest slice lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/50-choose-the-smallest-testable-slice/) gives the required proof gate, the false minimums and the stop rule.

interviews.title: Decide whether to split work across parallel workers
interviews.markdown:
Your manager wants a feature finished faster and suggests that you run two coding agents, or two engineers, in parallel on it. Tell me about a time you had to make that call. How did you decide, and what did you put in place before anyone started?

## Short answer

I delegate only when the work is really independent: two investigations that answer different unknowns, two implementations with disjoint files and contracts, a reviewer who only reads, or a slow external check that runs while local work continues. When the parts need the same files, the same open decision or the same mutable environment, I keep them serial, because a parallel split then converts one clear task into a coordination problem. Before anyone starts, each unit gets a goal, an owner, exclusive write paths, dependencies, a proof and a handoff.

## Full answer

### The parallelism test

More available workers is not a reason. The split is justified when at least one of these holds:

- two investigations can answer different unknowns on their own;
- two implementations own disjoint files and contracts;
- a reviewer can inspect a finished artifact without changing it;
- a slow external check can run while local work continues.

### A work unit is a contract

"Handle the backend" is not a unit. "Implement the duplicate check in one named file and prove it with the focused account test" is. Each unit records the goal, one accountable owner, exclusive paths, completed units it waits for, the exact evidence it returns, and a handoff with the files changed, the decisions made and the remaining risk.

### Three layers of isolation

1. Filesystem: separate worktrees or sandboxes stop accidental shared edits.
2. Ownership: the contract stops two workers from editing the same path on purpose.
3. State: separate logs and outputs stop one worker from overwriting another's evidence.

Filesystem isolation does not solve ownership. Two clean worktrees can still produce two conflicting designs. The merge contract has to settle shared interfaces before work begins.

### What the integrator does

The integrator confirms each handoff matches its scope, reads the proof output rather than the summary, combines changes in dependency order, runs the full cross-unit gate, rejects hidden scope growth, and records conflicts as new decisions instead of silent edits. If integration means rewriting most of a worker's result, the split was wrong.

### The call I made

The time this mattered most, the two halves looked independent but both needed the same response type to change. I ran one short unit to fix that contract first, then let the two implementations run in parallel against it. The serial step was shorter than the merge conflict it prevented.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** A docs unit asks to own the whole application directory. What happens? Expected: the plan is blocked, because that parent path overlaps the paths of the implementation unit.
- **Level 3:** A worker's dependency becomes invalid half way through. What is the rule? Expected: a written cancellation rule decided before the start, so the worker stops and returns a handoff instead of building on a dead contract.
- **Level 4:** Where does the human stay in the loop when agents do the work? Expected: on choices that change public behavior, risk, authority or irreversible cost; agents own bounded investigation, implementation, verification and review.
- **Level 4:** How do you know the decomposition was right after the fact? Expected: the integrator combined the handoffs without rewriting them, and the final changed-file set matched the union of the unit contracts.

## Wrong answers

- "Two agents are always faster than one." Parallel work saves wall time only when the pieces are independent; otherwise it raises the failure rate.
- "Separate worktrees solve the conflicts." They prevent accidental shared edits, not two conflicting designs of one interface.
- "The integrator fixes whatever does not fit." If most of a result must be rewritten at integration, the original split was the mistake.

## Taught in

The [delegation lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/45-delegate-with-isolation/) gives the parallelism test, the unit contract and the isolation layers.

interviews.title: Two users describe two different workflows
interviews.markdown:
Two senior analysts on the same team show you how they triage a flagged transaction. Their steps differ in order, in the tools they open, and in who they ask before they act. Your deadline allows one workflow in the first version. What do you do with the disagreement?

## Short answer

I keep both variants separate until I know why they differ. The difference can come from different roles, different risk levels, a legacy process next to a current one, a difference in expertise, or a real policy disagreement, and each of those leads to a different product. An averaged workflow can describe nobody, so the first version targets one variant on purpose and names the other as a known gap.

## Full answer

### Why not average

Two people can perform different workflows for good reasons. Merging their steps into one path produces a sequence that neither of them follows. The assistant then fails at the first handoff or exception, which is where these features fail most.

### What the difference can mean

| Cause | What it tells the build |
|---|---|
| Different roles | Two user types, maybe two outcome frames |
| Different risk levels | The branch is a feature, not noise |
| Legacy and current process | One variant may be retiring; confirm with the owner |
| Expertise difference | The expert path may be the target and the other the training gap |
| Policy disagreement | A human decision is needed before any build |

### How I resolve it

1. Record both variants as ordered steps with evidence and the rung of that evidence.
2. Find where the branch begins and which authority boundary each variant crosses.
3. Ask the owner of the process which cause applies; if it is a policy disagreement, that decision goes to a human and the build waits for it.
4. Pick one variant for the first slice by risk and frequency, and write the other as a non-goal with the reason.

### Where the exception hides

Often one analyst's "extra" step is the exception path the other analyst has stopped noticing. I ask for a real case where the normal path failed before I call a step optional.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** One analyst asks a supervisor before acting and the other does not. What is that step? Expected: an authority boundary; the build must respect it, and the two variants may differ in risk level or role.
- **Level 2:** You can only ship one path. How do you choose? Expected: by the risk and the frequency of each variant, with the other recorded as a named gap, not by averaging.
- **Level 3:** The owner says both are fine. What do you record? Expected: that the policy allows both, with the evidence, so the assistant does not force one on everybody.
- **Level 3:** How do you keep the second variant from disappearing from the plan? Expected: write it as a non-goal with its reason and a review point, so it stays visible as a decision instead of an omission.

## Wrong answers

- "Merge the two into one standard process." The averaged workflow may describe nobody and breaks at the handoff.
- "Follow the more senior person." Seniority is not evidence; the cause of the difference decides.
- "Treat the extra steps as optional and skip them." The extra step is often the exception path that carries most of the risk.

## Taught in

The [workflow discovery lesson](../../../phases/14-agent-engineering/48-discover-the-real-workflow/) explains why disagreement must not be averaged away and lists the causes behind variants.

interviews.title: Weight decay that went into the gradient
interviews.markdown:
A hand-written optimizer step is labeled AdamW. Review it:

```python
def adam_step(params, grad, m, v, t, lr, beta1, beta2, eps, weight_decay):
    grad = grad + weight_decay * params
    m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * grad
    v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * grad * grad
    m_hat = m / (1 - beta1 ** t)
    v_hat = v / (1 - beta2 ** t)
    return params - lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps), m, v
```

Is this AdamW? What changes, and why does it matter for a language model?

## Short answer

No, this is Adam with an L2 penalty folded into the gradient. AdamW applies the decay directly to the parameters, scaled by the learning rate, outside the adaptive step. When the penalty goes through the gradient it is divided by the second-moment estimate, so parameters with large gradients get almost no decay and the regularization becomes uneven across the model.

## Full answer

### The corrected step

```python
def adam_step(params, grad, m, v, t, lr, beta1, beta2, eps, weight_decay):
    m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * grad
    v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * grad * grad
    m_hat = m / (1 - beta1 ** t)
    v_hat = v / (1 - beta2 ** t)
    new = params - lr * (m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps) + weight_decay * params)
    return new, m, v
```

The decay term is added to the update, not to the gradient. It never passes through the moment estimates.

### What the difference changes

Adam normalizes every coordinate by its running gradient magnitude. A penalty that enters as part of the gradient is normalized too, so a weight with a large, noisy gradient is barely decayed while a weight with a tiny gradient is decayed hard. Decoupled decay shrinks every weight by the same fraction per step, which is what the regularizer was meant to do. Language model recipes use the decoupled form, and the loop in the training lesson builds its parameter groups around it.

### Three more details the practice pins

- The step counter starts at one. With `t = 0` the bias correction divides by zero, and with `t + 1` the first step acts as the second.
- Epsilon sits outside the square root. Inside it, tiny gradients give a much smaller step than intended.
- The function returns new state arrays. Updating `m` and `v` in place changes the caller's state and breaks checkpoint resume.

### Where the decay should not go

Even with the correct form, the decay belongs on matrix-shaped weights only. Normalization scales and biases get no decay, which is the subject of the parameter group split.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** What does the bias correction fix in the first steps? Expected: the moment estimates start at zero and are biased low early; dividing by `1 - beta**t` rescales them.
- **Level 2:** Why return new arrays instead of updating in place? Expected: a pure function keeps the caller's state intact, so a step can be retried or compared and a checkpoint stays consistent.
- **Level 3:** How does the learning rate schedule interact with decoupled decay? Expected: the decay is multiplied by the current learning rate, so warmup and cosine decay also scale the regularization over training.

## Wrong answers

- "L2 and weight decay are the same thing." They coincide for plain gradient descent, not for an adaptive optimizer that normalizes the gradient.
- "Put epsilon inside the square root for stability." It changes the step size for small gradients; the reference form adds it after the root.
- "Start the step counter at zero like an index." The bias correction then divides by zero on the first step.

## Taught in

The [training loop lesson](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/36-training-loop-eval/) configures AdamW with its decay split, the [cosine schedule lesson](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/44-cosine-lr-warmup/) pairs it with warmup and decay, and the [Adam practice](../../../practice/adam-step/) checks the decoupled form.

interviews.title: Train the smallest language model past its baseline
interviews.markdown:
Write a training loop for a table of next-character logits: one row per context character, one column per next character. Train it with gradient descent on a text, under a fixed step budget and a seeded generator, until its held-out NLL is lower than a model that ignores the context. Tell me what the held-out check must look like for the comparison to mean anything.

## Short answer

Build the pairs so that the current character is the context and the following character is the target, compute the log-softmax over each row, and descend the mean of the negative target log-probabilities over the training pairs within the step budget. The held-out check scores a fixed split that training never saw, with the same loss definition for the bigram and the unigram baseline, and the model only passes when its held-out value is lower than the baseline's. Reproducibility comes from drawing the initial table from the generator that the caller passes, not from a global one.

## Full answer

### The model and the loop

```python
def train(text, rng, steps, lr):
    pairs = [(ord(a), ord(b)) for a, b in zip(text, text[1:])]
    W = rng.normal(0, 1, (V, V))
    for _ in range(steps):
        logits = W[[a for a, _ in pairs]]
        logp = log_softmax(logits)
        grad = softmax(logits)
        grad[np.arange(len(pairs)), [b for _, b in pairs]] -= 1
        gW = np.zeros_like(W)
        np.add.at(gW, [a for a, _ in pairs], grad / len(pairs))
        W = W - lr * gW
    return W


def next_log_probs(W, context):
    return log_softmax(W[context])
```

The pair direction is the whole model: context first, target second. Reversing them trains a model that predicts the previous character, and counting each next character as its own context trains nothing about what follows what.

### The gradient sign

The update subtracts the gradient. Adding it climbs the loss, which is visible on the first evaluation, and is the first mutant the practice checks.

### The held-out check

The loop lesson's rule is that evaluation runs on a fixed held-out slice with no gradient, and the number must be comparable across runs. For this task that means three things. The split is fixed before training and never touched by the loop. The unigram baseline, which assigns each character its frequency in the training text regardless of context, is scored on the same held-out characters with the same loss definition. The bigram passes only when its held-out value is strictly lower. A model that wins on the training text and not on the held-out text has memorized the training text.

### The budget

A step budget is part of the contract. A loop that runs more steps than the budget may reach the target but fails the task, and in a real run it is the difference between a planned job and an overrun.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why return log-probabilities and not raw logits from the scoring function? Expected: the loss needs a normalized distribution per row; raw logits are not comparable across contexts.
- **Level 3:** The model beats the baseline on training text and loses on held-out text. What happened? Expected: it memorized the training pairs; a held-out split exists to catch exactly that.
- **Level 4:** How does this toy loop map onto the full training loop in the lesson? Expected: the pair construction is the shift-by-one, the row lookup is the forward, the held-out check is the fixed evaluation, and the budget is the step count of the schedule.

## Wrong answers

- "Evaluate on the training text to save time." The comparison then measures memorization and the baseline comparison means nothing.
- "Draw the initial table from the global random state." Two runs with one seed then differ, and the test for reproducibility fails.
- "Train until the loss stops improving." The budget is part of the contract and an open-ended loop hides a slow or stuck run.

## Taught in

The [training loop lesson](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/36-training-loop-eval/) sets the rules for held-out evaluation and loss alignment, and the [character bigram practice](../../../practice/train-char-bigram/) trains the smallest model under a step budget.

interviews.title: A merge that lets two matches share a symbol
interviews.markdown:
This function rewrites one word after a BPE merge was chosen. On the word `(7, 7, 7)` with the pair `(7, 7)` it returns `(300, 300, 7)`. Find the bug and give the correct output.

```python
def apply_merge(symbols, pair, new_id):
    out = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(symbols):
        if i + 1 < len(symbols) and symbols[i] == pair[0] and symbols[i + 1] == pair[1]:
            out.append(new_id)
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(symbols[i])
            i += 1
    return tuple(out)
```

## Short answer

After a match the scan moves one position instead of two, so the second symbol of the match is read again: it starts the next match or is copied to the output. Matches must not share a symbol. The correct result is `(300, 7)`: the first two sevens become one new id and the third seven stays.

## Full answer

### What the bug does

With a step of one after a match, the scan sees the pair at positions zero and one, emits the new id, and then looks at positions one and two, which also match. The word gains a symbol it never had, so the merged corpus is wrong and every later step counts pairs on corrupted words. Encoding at inference reuses the same function, so every text with a repeated symbol decodes to different bytes than it was given.

### The fix

```python
        if i + 1 < len(symbols) and symbols[i] == pair[0] and symbols[i + 1] == pair[1]:
            out.append(new_id)
            i += 2
```

Scan from left to right and continue after the second symbol of the match. The merge loop in the tokenizers chapter is exactly this, and the practice task has a mutant for the single step that fails on `[a, a, a]`.

### Why the left-to-right rule matters

Non-overlapping replacement from the left is a convention, and the training loop and the encoder must share it. If training merged from the left and the encoder merged from the right, the same word would get different ids in training and at inference. The merge table only works when both sides apply it the same way.

### A related check

The function returns a new tuple. It must not write into the caller's sequence, because the training loop still holds the old corpus while it builds the new one.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** What does the same bug do to the pair counts of the next training step? Expected: it counts pairs that do not exist in the real corpus, so later merges are chosen on wrong numbers.
- **Level 2:** Give an input where the bug produces a correct answer. Expected: only a word with no match for the pair, such as `(7, 8, 7)` with `(7, 7)`; every match leaves an extra copy of its second symbol.
- **Level 3:** How does a round-trip test catch this bug? Expected: encode a string with a repeated byte, decode the ids, and compare the bytes; the extra merged symbol expands to more bytes than the input had.

## Wrong answers

- "Replace the pair with a string method on the joined symbols." Ids are integers, not characters, and joining them hides the boundaries between ids.
- "Match from the right instead." Either direction works alone, but training and inference must use the same one; left-to-right is the convention.
- "Return a list instead of a tuple to make it faster." The words are dictionary keys and must stay hashable.

## Taught in

The [tokenizers lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/01-tokenizers/) writes the merge loop with the two-position step, the [BPE from scratch lesson](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/30-bpe-tokenizer-from-scratch/) explains the shared merge contract, and the [BPE practice](../../../practice/bpe-merge-step/) tests the overlap case.

interviews.title: Train a BPE merge list from word counts
interviews.markdown:
You get a corpus as a dictionary from words, each a tuple of byte ids, to the number of times the word occurs. Write the training loop that produces an ordered list of merges, and state the three rules that make the loop deterministic. Then tell me what the loop must not do to the caller's data.

## Short answer

Each step counts every adjacent pair inside each word, weighted by the word frequency, picks the pair with the highest count, rewrites every occurrence of that pair into one new id, and records the merge. The three rules are: pairs never cross a word boundary, ties go to the smallest pair in tuple order, and the loop stops when no pair repeats. The input dictionary and its tuples are never changed; the loop builds a new corpus each step.

## Full answer

### The loop

```python
def train(units, num_merges, first_id=256):
    merges = []
    units = dict(units)
    for i in range(num_merges):
        pairs = count_pairs(units)
        best = best_pair(pairs)
        if best is None or pairs[best] < 2:
            break
        new_id = first_id + i
        units = {apply_merge(word, best, new_id): freq for word, freq in units.items()}
        merges.append((best, new_id))
    return merges, units
```

The first ids are reserved for the raw bytes, so the first merge gets the next free id and each later merge gets the next one. The merge list in training order is the tokenizer. Encoding fresh text applies the same merges in the same order, so a change of order at inference decodes a different stream of ids.

### Weighted counts

A pair inside a word that occurs five times adds five to the count, not one. Counting each occurrence once makes rare long words outvote common short ones, and the merge order changes. Pairs do not cross from the end of one word to the start of the next; the word split is what keeps merges inside words and lets them generalize.

### Ties and the stop rule

Two pairs with the same count must resolve the same way on every run, so the smallest pair in tuple order wins. Without a fixed rule, dictionary order decides and two training runs on the same corpus produce different tokenizers. The loop stops early when the best count is below two, because a pair that occurs once does not compress anything and only spends vocabulary slots.

### Do not change the input

The caller's dictionary and tuples stay as they were. Clearing and refilling the dictionary in place, or rewriting tuples through a list, changes data the caller may still use. Each step builds a new dictionary from the merged words.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why does the symbol count fall as training proceeds, and what does that do to the cost of a step? Expected: each merge shortens words, so the pair count over the corpus shrinks and later steps are cheaper.
- **Level 2:** What does the tie rule protect? Expected: reproducibility; the same corpus must give the same merge list on every machine.
- **Level 3:** Two words merge into the same tuple after a step. What must the new dictionary do? Expected: add their frequencies together instead of keeping only the last one.
- **Level 3:** How does the vocabulary size relate to the number of merges? Expected: the base byte block plus one id per merge, plus any reserved special ids.

## Wrong answers

- "Count each pair once per word." Frequency weighting is what makes common pairs win early.
- "Take the first pair with the maximum count." Dictionary order is not stable across inputs, so the tokenizer becomes irreproducible.
- "Keep merging until the budget is spent." A pair that appears once gains nothing and wastes vocabulary.

## Taught in

The [BPE from scratch lesson](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/30-bpe-tokenizer-from-scratch/) gives the training loop and the merge table contract, the [tokenizers lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/01-tokenizers/) walks a merge sequence by hand, and the [BPE practice](../../../practice/bpe-merge-step/) checks the tie rule and the stop rule.

interviews.title: A causal mask that blocks the token itself
interviews.markdown:
A decoder's attention returns a zero vector in the first row of every sequence. The mask code is:

```python
def causal_mask(T):
    return np.triu(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool), k=0)

weights = softmax(scores)
weights[mask] = 0
out = weights @ V
```

Two things are wrong. Find both and explain what each one does to the output.

## Short answer

The mask uses a diagonal offset of zero, so every token blocks itself and the first token has no allowed key, which leaves an empty row. The mask is also applied after the softmax, so the rows no longer sum to one. Build the mask with an offset of one, and set the blocked scores to a very negative value before the softmax.

## Full answer

### Bug one: the diagonal

A causal mask lets position `i` see positions zero through `i`, itself included. `np.triu` with `k=0` keeps the diagonal in the blocked set. For the first query every key is blocked, so this code sets the whole first row of weights to zero and the first output row is zero. If you only move the mask before the softmax and fill with negative infinity, that row has nothing to normalize and the division produces NaN. Use `k=1` so the diagonal stays visible.

### Bug two: masking after the softmax

Setting weights to zero after normalization leaves each row summing to less than one, by exactly the mass that the future keys received. The output then shrinks and the model trains against a moving scale. The mask must act on the scores before the softmax, by setting blocked entries to a very negative value, so that their exponentials are zero and the remaining entries renormalize.

### The corrected code

```python
def causal_mask(T):
    return np.triu(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool), k=1)

scores = np.where(mask, -1e9, scores)
weights = softmax(scores)
out = weights @ V
```

### Why both bugs can pass a shape test

Neither bug changes a shape. Only a check of the weights, or a check that the first output row is not zero, exposes them. The practice task checks the causal weights against a reference and includes the first row.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why a very negative number and not negative infinity? Expected: infinity works in most frameworks, but a fully masked row then produces NaN, while a finite value keeps the arithmetic defined.
- **Level 2:** How does the mask interact with the batch dimension? Expected: the mask is tokens by tokens and broadcasts across batches and heads; it is built once per sequence length.
- **Level 3:** The same model is used for prefill and then one token at a time. Does the mask change? Expected: at decode time the single query sees every cached key, so no mask is needed for that step; the causal rule was already applied when those keys were produced.
- **Level 3:** A padding mask and a causal mask must both apply. How do you combine them? Expected: combine the boolean masks with a logical or before the scores are masked, so a padded key is blocked for every query.

## Wrong answers

- "Set the blocked weights to zero and renormalize the rows." It works numerically but doubles the work; masking the scores before the softmax does the renormalization for free.
- "The first token should attend to nothing." The first token must attend to itself; an empty row has no valid distribution.
- "Use a lower-triangular ones matrix as the mask." A ones matrix marks the allowed entries, so it must be inverted before it is used as a blocked-entry mask.

## Taught in

The [self-attention lesson](../../../phases/07-transformers-deep-dive/02-self-attention-from-scratch/) asks for the mask as its first exercise, and the [attention practice](../../../practice/scaled-dot-product-attention/) tests the first row of the masked weights.

interviews.title: Which parameters get weight decay
interviews.markdown:
A training run looks healthy for the first few thousand steps, then the loss starts to climb and samples degrade. The optimizer is built with one parameter group:

```python
optimizer = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)
```

Write the function that builds the parameter groups correctly and explain which tensors must be excluded from decay and why.

## Short answer

Decay belongs on matrix-shaped tensors, which are the linear weights and the embedding tables, and not on normalization scales or biases. A decayed LayerNorm scale drifts toward zero over thousands of steps until normalization stops working, which matches the late failure. Split the parameters by shape into a decay group and a no-decay group and pass both to the optimizer.

## Full answer

### The split

```python
def build_param_groups(model, weight_decay):
    decay, no_decay = [], []
    for name, p in model.named_parameters():
        if not p.requires_grad:
            continue
        (decay if p.dim() >= 2 else no_decay).append(p)
    return [
        {"params": decay, "weight_decay": weight_decay},
        {"params": no_decay, "weight_decay": 0},
    ]
```

A two-dimensional or larger tensor is a weight matrix or an embedding table. A one-dimensional tensor is a scale or a shift, which includes LayerNorm parameters and every bias. The rule by dimension is simple and matches the standard recipe.

### Why decay on a scale is harmful

Weight decay pulls every decayed parameter toward zero on every step. A linear weight has gradient pressure in many directions and the pull acts as regularization. A LayerNorm scale has one job, to set the magnitude of the normalized activations, and a steady pull toward zero shrinks the residual stream of every block until the signal is too small for the layers that follow. The effect accumulates slowly, which is why the run looks fine at first.

### Why decay on a bias is waste

Decaying a bias is mathematically harmless but spends update cycles on a parameter that regularization does not need to control. The split excludes it along with the scales.

### How to test the split

A unit test can walk the named parameters and assert that each scale and bias landed in the no-decay group and each linear and embedding weight landed in the decay group. The loop lesson lists exactly this test as its first exercise.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** The language model head is tied to the token embedding. Which group is it in, and how many times? Expected: once, in the decay group, because it is the same tensor as the embedding table.
- **Level 3:** A model uses RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm. Does the rule change? Expected: no; the RMSNorm weight is one-dimensional and stays out of the decay group.
- **Level 4:** Why does the problem appear late rather than at the start of training? Expected: the decay shrinks the scale by a small fraction per step, so the damage compounds over thousands of steps before the activations become too small.

## Wrong answers

- "Weight decay applies to all weights by definition." The standard recipe excludes normalization and bias tensors; applying it everywhere breaks normalization over time.
- "Decide by parameter name, excluding anything called bias." Names vary across implementations; the dimension rule is robust.
- "Lower the weight decay until the run is stable." A smaller value slows the drift but keeps the pull on the scales.

## Taught in

The [training loop lesson](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/36-training-loop-eval/) defines the two-group AdamW split and the test for it, and the [Adam practice](../../../practice/adam-step/) implements the decoupled decay the groups feed into.

interviews.title: Dropout that still acts during evaluation
interviews.markdown:
Two evaluation runs on the same checkpoint and the same fixed validation batches report different losses. The dropout layer is:

```python
def dropout_forward(x, p, rng, training):
    mask = rng.random(x.shape) >= p
    if training:
        return x * mask / (1 - p), mask
    return x * (1 - p), mask
```

Find every problem with the inference path and explain what the evaluation function expects.

## Short answer

Inverted dropout scales the kept units during training so that inference is the identity, but this inference path multiplies the input by one minus p, which belongs to the non-inverted form and shrinks every activation. It also draws from the generator in inference mode, which changes every later random number in the run, such as the next training mask and the next probe sample. Inference must return the input unchanged and must not touch the generator.

## Full answer

### The two bugs

1. Scaling at inference. With inverted dropout the division by one minus p happens in training, so the expected activation already matches the no-dropout value. Scaling again at inference halves the signal at a rate of one half and damages every layer that follows.
2. Drawing at inference. The mask is sampled before the branch. Evaluation consumes random numbers, so the generation sample after the probe, and any later training step, sees a different stream than a run without the probe.

### The fix

```python
def dropout_forward(x, p, rng, training):
    if not training:
        return x.copy(), np.ones(x.shape, dtype=bool)
    mask = rng.random(x.shape) >= p
    return x * mask / (1 - p), mask
```

At inference the layer returns a copy of the input and a mask that is true everywhere, and it does not draw. Keep an entry when the random number is at or above p, so the complement rule is right, and divide the kept entries by one minus p. The backward pass multiplies the incoming gradient by the same mask and divides by the same factor.

### What evaluation expects

The training loop's evaluation function runs a fixed number of validation batches with no gradient and no dropout, and the number must be reproducible across runs given the same seed and split. Any randomness inside the model during that pass breaks the comparison between two runs, because the difference measures the random stream rather than the model. The assembly lesson's model has an embedding dropout of 0.1, so this layer sits in the path of every evaluation.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why divide by one minus p during training at all? Expected: so the expected value of each activation is the same with and without the mask, which makes inference the identity.
- **Level 2:** Why must the backward pass use the same mask? Expected: the gradient must flow only through the units that were kept, with the same scale, otherwise the gradient does not match the forward computation.
- **Level 3:** The evaluation is reproducible but still differs from a run that skipped the probe. What else draws? Expected: the sampled generation at the probe step consumes draws from the shared generator; give the probe its own generator.

## Wrong answers

- "Scale down at inference as the original dropout paper did." That form skips the scaling in training; mixing the two forms shrinks the activations.
- "Re-seed the generator before every evaluation." It hides the extra draws but still changes the training stream afterwards; the inference path should not draw at all.
- "Keep an entry when the random number is below p." That keeps a fraction p and drops the rest, the complement of the intended mask.

## Taught in

The [training loop lesson](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/36-training-loop-eval/) requires that evaluation skip gradients and dropout, the [GPT assembly lesson](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/35-gpt-model-assembly/) places the embedding dropout, and the [inverted dropout practice](../../../practice/inverted-dropout/) checks the identity at inference.

interviews.title: Convert a multi-head checkpoint to grouped-query heads
interviews.markdown:
You have a trained model with 64 query heads and 64 key and value heads, and you want to serve it with 8 key and value heads to shrink the cache. Write the function that pools the key projection of the checkpoint into groups, say by what factor the cache memory for keys and values falls, and explain why the pooled model needs more training before it is usable.

## Short answer

Group `g` of the new projection is the mean of the consecutive heads `g r` to `g r + r - 1`, where `r` is the number of query heads per group, taken over the columns of the projection matrix. The cache holds keys and values for 8 heads instead of 64, so that memory falls by a factor of eight. The mean of several heads is not a head the model was trained with, so quality drops until a short continued training run adapts the query heads to their shared group.

## Full answer

### The pooling

```python
def mean_pool_kv_heads(w, n_heads, n_kv_heads):
    if n_heads % n_kv_heads:
        raise ValueError("query heads must be a multiple of kv heads")
    D, cols = w.shape
    d_head = cols // n_heads
    r = n_heads // n_kv_heads
    grouped = w.reshape(D, n_kv_heads, r, d_head)
    return grouped.mean(axis=2).reshape(D, n_kv_heads * d_head)
```

The reshape puts the groups first and the heads inside a group next, because the heads of one group are consecutive blocks of columns. Reshaping as `(D, r, G, d_head)` pools heads that are `G` apart, which gives a correct shape with the wrong groups. The mean, not the sum, keeps the scale of the projected keys close to the original, so the attention scores stay in range.

### The memory factor

The cache stores one key and one value vector per layer, per head, per token. The number of query heads does not enter. Going from 64 to 8 key and value heads divides the stored bytes per token by eight, which is the example the multi-head lesson gives for a large open model. Weights fall much less, because the query and output projections are unchanged and only the key and value projections shrink.

### Why it needs training

The query heads were trained against their own key heads. After pooling, eight query heads read one averaged key head that none of them saw in training. The lesson's lineage describes converting multi-head checkpoints to grouped-query checkpoints as a recipe with a continued training step; the pooling gives a starting point close to the original, and the uptraining recovers most of the quality. Serving the pooled weights directly works, but the eval must be rerun before shipping.

### What does not change

The head size, the query projection, the output projection and the attention function itself are the same. Only the key and value projections and the repeat inside attention change, so the rest of the loader and the block are untouched.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why pool consecutive heads and not every eighth head? Expected: the attention reads group `h` floor-divided by `r` for query head `h`, so the pooled heads must be the ones that will share a group.
- **Level 4:** How does the cache saving change when the model is served with a longer context? Expected: it does not change as a factor; the saving is per token, so the absolute bytes saved grow with the number of tokens held.
- **Level 4:** The multi-head latent variant compresses keys and values into a low-rank latent. What does it trade for the extra saving? Expected: compute, because the latent must be projected back to full keys and values at attention time.

## Wrong answers

- "Pooling is lossless since the mean preserves the average key." The individual heads are lost; the queries were trained against them, so quality drops until the model is adapted.
- "The cache shrinks by the ratio of query heads to total heads." Only key and value heads live in the cache; the factor is the old count of key and value heads over the new count.
- "Sum the heads so no information is lost." The sum scales the keys by the group size and pushes the scores out of the range the softmax was trained for.

## Taught in

The [multi-head attention lesson](../../../phases/07-transformers-deep-dive/03-multi-head-attention/) gives the grouped-query lineage and the cache factor, and the [grouped-query practice](../../../practice/grouped-query-attention/) implements the pooling of a multi-head checkpoint.

interviews.title: GQA that pairs query heads with the wrong group
interviews.markdown:
A GQA implementation repeats the key and value heads up to the query head count with this line, where `kv` has shape batch, groups, tokens, head size:

```python
kv_full = np.tile(kv, (1, n_heads // n_kv_heads, 1, 1))
```

The shapes match and the outputs are wrong for every configuration with more than one group. Explain which query head ends up with which group, and write the correct expansion.

## Short answer

Tiling repeats the whole block of groups, so query head `h` reads group `h` modulo the number of groups. The convention is that consecutive query heads share a group: head `h` reads group `h` floor-divided by the repeat factor. Repeat each group in place along the head axis instead of tiling the block.

## Full answer

### The two layouts

With four query heads and two groups the repeat factor is two. The correct expansion gives the sequence of groups `0, 0, 1, 1`: the first two query heads share group zero and the next two share group one. Tiling gives `0, 1, 0, 1`, so heads one and two swap partners. Every head still has a key and value tensor of the right shape, which is why no shape check fails, but half the heads attend with the wrong keys.

### The fix

```python
def repeat_kv(kv, n_heads):
    B, G, T, d_head = kv.shape
    if n_heads % G:
        raise ValueError("query heads must be a multiple of kv heads")
    r = n_heads // G
    return np.repeat(kv, r, axis=1)
```

`np.repeat` along the group axis copies each group `r` times next to itself, which produces the floor-division mapping. The divisibility check belongs here, because a non-integer repeat factor silently truncates and drops heads.

### Why the mapping is a convention and not a choice

The projection weights of a trained checkpoint were learned under one mapping. The multi-head lesson describes the lineage: multi-head attention with one group per head, multi-query attention with a single shared group, and the grouped form in between with the first `r` heads on group zero. A model converted from multi-head weights by pooling consecutive heads only works if attention reads the groups in the same consecutive order.

### Why it exists

Only `G` key and value heads live in the cache instead of `H`, so the cache shrinks by the factor `H / G` while quality stays close to standard multi-head attention. The lesson's example is a large open model that pairs 64 query heads against only 8 shared groups.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** With one group, what does the function compute? Expected: multi-query attention; every query head shares the single key and value head.
- **Level 3:** Where does the scale factor come from after the repeat? Expected: the square root of the head size, the same as in multi-head attention; dividing by the square root of the full width is a separate common bug.
- **Level 4:** How does a framework avoid materializing the repeated copies? Expected: it broadcasts the group axis inside the attention kernel, or the attention call accepts fewer key and value heads directly, so memory holds only the groups.

## Wrong answers

- "Tile and repeat give the same result when the shapes match." They give different head-to-group assignments; only one matches the trained weights.
- "Average the groups and use one key tensor for all heads." That turns the model into multi-query attention with weights it was not trained for.
- "The mapping does not matter because attention is permutation invariant." Attention is invariant over keys within a head, not over which key head a query head reads.

## Taught in
