- "The acceptance length is fine, so speculation is working." It measures the draft's guesses, not the server; on the L4 each token came 1.6 to 2.3 times faster at every load and the server delivered no more tokens per second from 32 users.
- "Random prompts are real text, so the benchmark is realistic." The random set cuts or repeats the first turn of ShareGPT conversations to 512 tokens with the end token ignored; on GSM8K and code prompts speculation gave 1.6 times the output at 32 users, and on ShareGPT it gave none.
- "Raise --max-running-requests to let more users in." On the L4 the pool held about 15 requests, so a higher cap changes nothing; the pool was the limit, and the draft took nearly 60 percent of it.
- "Use NGRAM instead, it needs no draft weights." It helped only on GSM8K and code, by about 1.1 to 1.2 times at 8 users, and on the other two sets it was slower with a P99 ITL of 244 to 779 ms.

## Taught in

[The SGLang speculative decoding section](../../../manuals/sglang-101/sections/4-4-speculative-decoding.md) has the L4 and GB10 sweeps and the four-dataset test.

interviews.title: Temperature zero gave two different answers
interviews.markdown:
You run the same evaluation twice at temperature 0 on a serving engine and the scores differ. You send one failing prompt alone and get one answer, then send it inside a busy batch and get another. Nothing in the request changed. Explain what did change, and what a seed can and cannot fix.

## Short answer

The batch changed the arithmetic. Floating-point addition is not associative, and the kernels split their sums by the batch size, so the same request adds its numbers in a different order in a batch of 3 than in a batch of 30; a change in the last bit can flip the top logit, and every later token then follows a different text. The prefix cache does the same, because a request that reuses cached blocks runs a different prefill path, and so does the dtype. A seed fixes only the random draws of sampling, so it is not enough: offline, run the engine in one process with the same order; online, use the batch-invariant mode and pay its speed cost.

## Full answer

### Four things that change one request

- **The batch.** Matrix multiplies, softmax and norms split their sums into tiles, and many kernels pick the split from the batch size.
- **The schedule.** In a multiprocess server, the timing of requests decides which batch each one joins.
- **The prefix cache.** A request that reuses cached blocks computes its prompt in a different way than a request with no hit.
- **The dtype.** BF16 and FP16 round each number differently, so the same model writes different text in the two.

The vLLM seed defaults to 0 and cannot be unset, because speculative decoding needs every worker to sample the same tokens. So a seed is always there, and it is not enough by itself.

### What the manual counted

Greedy outputs of Qwen3-0.6B, 32 ShareGPT questions after one shared system prompt of about 170 tokens, 128 output tokens, compared token by token between two runs. The number in brackets is the median position of the first token that differs:

| Comparison | SGLang | vLLM |
|---|---|---|
| flushed repeat against fresh | 0 of 32 | 0 of 32 |
| cache off against cache off | 0 of 32 | 0 of 32 |
| fresh against warm cache | 21 of 32 (45) | 11 of 32 (57) |
| cache on against cache off | 25 of 32 (26) | 21 of 32 (48) |

At one user and the same cache state, the text repeated exactly. A warm cache changed 21 of 32 outputs on SGLang and 11 of 32 on vLLM. At 64 users sent at once, two runs with the cache off still differed, in 27 of 64 outputs on SGLang and 50 of 64 on vLLM: the batch alone changed most outputs. BF16 against FP16 at one user changed 48 of 64 outputs on vLLM and 51 of 64 on SGLang for the 0.6B model, and 56 and 57 of 64 for Qwen3-1.7B.

The SGLang probe on the GB10 makes the point in one prompt. Sent five times alone and five times inside a batch of 16 at temperature 0, the default server wrote two texts, which parted after 238 characters. The first request alone had computed its prompt from nothing; the four later ones found it in the radix cache. With deterministic mode on, all ten requests wrote the same text.

### What fixes it

| Case | Fix | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Offline evals with the `LLM` class | `VLLM_ENABLE_V1_MULTIPROCESSING=0`, the same seed, the same prompts in the same order | the engine runs in your process, so the schedule repeats |
| A live server | `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, or `--enable-deterministic-inference` on SGLang | slower kernels for every request |
| Greedy evals that must match exactly | greedy sampling plus one of the two above | as above |

Every fix also needs the same hardware, the same engine version and the same settings. On SGLang the flag replaces the matrix, softmax, norm and batched-multiply operators with batch-invariant kernels, forces the plain sampler, fixes the all-reduce order under tensor parallelism, accepts only some attention backends, turns the radix cache off unless the backend supports it, and gives every request without a `sampling_seed` the seed 42.

### How to test it

Run the same eval twice and compare the outputs token by token, not only the score. Flush the prefix cache or restart the server before each probe. If the outputs differ, take one prompt that differs and run it alone twice. If the two answers match when alone, and the batched probe started from the same cache state, the batch causes the difference. SGLang ships a test that sends one prompt in random batch sizes and counts distinct outputs, with modes for a single prompt, shared prefixes and cached against uncached prefill.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Which comparisons in the manual's table gave the same text every time? Expected: a repeat after a cache flush against a fresh run, and a repeat with the cache off against the cache off, both 0 of 32 changed on both engines.
- **Level 3:** Why can a warm prefix cache change a greedy answer when the model and the prompt are the same? Expected: a request that reuses cached blocks computes its prompt in a different path than a full prefill, so the logits differ in their last bits, and one changed token changes the rest; it changed 21 of 32 outputs on SGLang and 11 of 32 on vLLM.
- **Level 4:** Under load two cache-off runs still differed. What does that say about the fix? Expected: the batch alone changed most outputs, 50 of 64 on vLLM, so a cache reset is enough only at one user; a live server needs batch-invariant kernels, and the manual did not test that mode at that load.

## Wrong answers

- "Temperature 0 makes the output deterministic." Greedy picks the top logit, and the batch changes the logits in their last bits; the GB10 server gave two texts for one prompt at temperature 0 with nothing in the request changed.
- "Set a seed and the outputs match." The seed only fixes the random draws; the vLLM seed defaults to 0 and cannot be unset, and the outputs still changed with the batch and the cache.
- "Flush the cache before each run and you are done." At one user that was enough, 0 of 32 changed; at 64 users two runs with the cache off still differed in 50 of 64 outputs, because the batch changed the sums.
- "Switch to FP16 for exact results." BF16 and FP16 round differently, so the same model writes different text in the two dtypes, 48 of 64 outputs for the 0.6B model; keep one dtype between runs you compare.

## Taught in

[Get reproducible outputs](../../../manuals/vllm-101/sections/3-8-get-reproducible-outputs.md) and [the SGLang deterministic inference section](../../../manuals/sglang-101/sections/4-6-deterministic-inference-and-logprobs.md) count the changed outputs and list the fixes.

interviews.title: Choose tensor, pipeline or data parallelism
interviews.markdown:
You have a model that does not fit on one GPU, or you need more throughput than one GPU gives. Walk me through how you choose between tensor, pipeline and data parallelism, and what each one costs in communication.

## Short answer

Ask three questions. If the model fits on one GPU with room for the KV cache you need, use data parallelism, one full copy per GPU, and the output grows with the copies. If it does not fit, split it: tensor parallelism inside one machine when the GPUs have a fast link and the GPU count divides the attention heads, and pipeline parallelism when they do not or when the model needs more than one machine. Tensor parallelism talks after every layer, pipeline parallelism once per stage boundary, and data parallelism not at all between copies.

## Full answer

### Three questions

| Question | If yes | If no |
|---|---|---|
| Does the model fit on one GPU, with room for the KV cache you need? | Data parallelism: one copy per GPU, `--data-parallel-size N`. | Split the model; the next question decides where. |
| Does the split model fit inside one machine? | Keep the split inside the machine; the next question picks the layout. | Add pipeline parallelism across machines. |
| Do the GPUs have NVLink, and does the GPU count divide the model evenly? | Tensor parallelism, `--tensor-parallel-size N`. | Pipeline parallelism inside the machine, `--pipeline-parallel-size N`. |

Across machines: set the pipeline size to the number of machines and the tensor size to the GPUs in each machine. The tensor size must divide the attention-head count. If the GPUs in a machine do not divide it, use a tensor size of 1 and put the whole GPU count into the pipeline size.

### What each layout costs

| Layout | What it splits | Communication | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tensor | each layer across GPUs | after every layer, so it needs a fast link | a model too big for one GPU, inside one machine |
| Pipeline | the layers into stages | once per stage boundary | a model too big for one machine, or GPUs without a fast link |
| Data | nothing, each GPU holds a copy | none between copies | more output from a model that fits |
| Expert | the experts of a mixture-of-experts model | before and after the expert layers | large expert models |

Tensor parallelism also splits the KV cache, so each GPU has more room for it. When the weights fill most of one GPU, two GPUs can hold several times the pool of one. The exception is a model with multi-head latent attention: it stores one compressed latent per token that cannot be split across heads, so every tensor-parallel rank keeps the full cache and more ranks add no tokens. Attention data parallelism answers that case.

### Check the link

Tensor parallelism sends data after every layer. On GPUs joined only by PCIe, such as two L4s in one host, that traffic can cost more than the split saves. The vLLM documentation suggests pipeline parallelism on such a machine, because it sends data only at stage boundaries, and it also accepts a GPU count that does not divide the model evenly. The manual did not run either layout on its two L4s, so measure them against each other before you pick.

### Start a second machine

Run the collective test script on both machines first. When the network and the drivers work, each process prints its success lines. Then start the server with a launcher that spans the machines, and start the API on one machine only. The traffic between the machines is not encrypted and can run code on the other side, so keep it on a private network.

### Count the processes

With data parallelism vLLM starts one engine core per copy and one coordinator that keeps them in step. With tensor parallelism it starts one worker per GPU under one engine core. In SGLang the world size is `--tp-size` times `--pp-size`, and `--dp-size` copies get a controller that sends each request to one copy, round robin by default. That controller does not look at pools or queues. On the manual's two L4s, where one card was shared and its copy had a pool of 2,925 tokens against 24,094, the pair served less than one card at every load.

### Give a tensor group whole GPUs

Before SGLang loads weights for a tensor group, each rank measures its free memory and the group keeps the smallest value. If that value is under 90 percent of the local free memory, the server stops. On the shared pair the second card had 18.28 GB free against the 19.53 GB that the check required, so `--tp-size 2` refused to start, and no flag turns the check off. Every rank holds the same share of weights and the same pool, so the smallest card sets the size for all of them.

### Very long prompts

For prompts of hundreds of thousands of tokens, vLLM can split one sequence across GPUs with context parallelism. Use it when one long request is the problem, not when many short ones are.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Two GPUs in one host joined by PCIe only, and the model fits on one. What do you run? Expected: data parallelism, two full copies, because nothing moves between copies; tensor parallelism would pay after every layer over the slow link.
- **Level 3:** The model needs two machines of 8 GPUs. How do you set the sizes, and what do you check first? Expected: pipeline size 2 for the machines and tensor size 8 inside each, with 8 dividing the attention heads; run the collective test on both machines first and keep the traffic on a private network, because it is not encrypted.
- **Level 3:** Tensor parallelism on two GPUs where one is shared with another job. What does SGLang do at startup? Expected: it measures free memory on each rank, keeps the smallest, and stops if that is under 90 percent of the local free memory, because every rank holds the same share and pool; give the group whole GPUs.
- **Level 4:** Why does tensor parallelism add no KV capacity when the attention keeps one latent per token? Expected: that attention stores one compressed latent per token that cannot be split across heads, so every rank keeps the full cache; attention data parallelism gives each group its own requests and cache, so capacity grows with the groups.

## Wrong answers

- "Tensor parallelism is the default way to use more GPUs." It is the way to make a model fit; when the model fits, data parallelism adds output with no traffic between copies, and tensor parallelism over PCIe can cost more than it saves.
- "More copies always mean more throughput." Only when every copy has about the same pool; a pair where one copy had an eighth of the pool served less than one card, because the round-robin controller fed it half the requests.
- "Pipeline parallelism is only for several machines." Inside one machine it is the choice when the GPUs lack a fast link or when the GPU count does not divide the model evenly.
- "Any GPU count works with tensor parallelism." The size must divide the attention-head count of the model; otherwise use a tensor size of 1 and put the whole count into the pipeline size.

## Taught in

[Choose tensor, pipeline, or data parallelism](../../../manuals/vllm-101/sections/6-1-choose-tensor-pipeline-or-data-parallelism.md) gives the decision tree, and [the SGLang parallelism section](../../../manuals/sglang-101/sections/6-1-tp-size-dp-size-and-attn-dp-size.md) adds the memory balance check and the unequal pair.

interviews.title: Two clients, two numbers, one server
interviews.markdown:
Two engineers benchmark the same server on the same day and report numbers that differ by a few percent. Both used standard benchmark clients. Before you look at the server, what about the clients could explain the gap, and what rules would you set for the team?

## Short answer

The client is part of the measurement. On one vLLM server the SGLang client read a median first token 3 to 10 percent higher and an output throughput 2 to 8 percent lower than the vLLM client, the two clients sent different random prompts, and temperature 0.7 raised the time per token by 10 to 13 percent at one user against temperature 0. The rules: one client, one temperature, one prompt length distribution with the range ratio stated, a flush and a new seed per run, the clock recorded, and all of that written next to every number.

## Full answer

### Three clients on one server

The manual ran the SGLang client, `vllm bench serve` and its Rust version against one vLLM server with Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B, with a cache reset before every run and the clients alternated over two rounds. Output tokens per second at 64 users:

| Temperature | SGLang client | vllm bench | vllm bench, Rust |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 359, 348 | 379, 377 | 371, 365 |
| 0.7 | 331, 343 | 360, 363 | 356, 353 |

The two vLLM clients agreed within the noise at 1, 16 and 64 users. The SGLang client read a slower server: a median first token 3 to 10 percent higher, and at 16 and 64 users an output throughput 2 to 8 percent lower. The two clients send different prompt tokens from their random datasets, so part of a small gap can come from the prompts. Temperature 0.7 raised the median time per token over temperature 0 by 10 to 13 percent at one user and 3 to 6 percent at 16 and 64 users.

### Four defaults that change the result

The SGLang client makes choices before it measures anything:

| Setting | Default | What it does to the result |
|---|---|---|
| `--random-range-ratio` | 0.0 | each length is drawn from 1 to the length you asked for, so the average prompt is about half of it |
| `ignore_eos` | on | every request generates exactly the output length you asked for |
| `--request-rate` | inf | all requests are sent at time 0, and only the concurrency cap holds them back |
| `--warmup-requests` | 1 | one request runs before the clock starts |

The first row is the trap. With the default ratio, an input length of 512 gives an average prompt near 256 tokens, and the report says 512. Pass 1.0 or write the length distribution next to the result. With 1.0, 32 prompts of 512 tokens give an input total of 16384 in the report.

### Fixed lengths form waves

With the ratio at 1.0 every request has the same length, so requests that start together finish together and their replacements arrive together. At 16 users on the L4, fixed lengths gave a median time to first token of 1,996 ms and a P99 ITL of 82 ms; mixed lengths gave 291 ms and 300 ms. The two settings measure two different servers. Fixed lengths measure bursts, with a slow first token and smooth tokens. Mixed lengths measure steady traffic, with a fast first token and stalls in the stream. Keep 1.0 to compare two builds, and run your real length mix before you set a latency target.

### The client's own queue

The SGLang client sends every request from one Python process. A 2026 study found that such a client adds its own queue at high request rates and then reports a first token and a time per token higher than the server gave. Before you trust a number at a high rate, compare one client process with two processes that each send half the rate. The lesson names the same trap for a general load tester: tokenization under the interpreter lock in the client inflates the reported inter-token latency, and one prompt sent in a loop hits the prefix cache on almost every request and inflates the throughput.

### Hand-written scripts

One report measured 13 tokens per second for a large model on eight GPUs against 60 from a hosted API. The script counted words split on spaces and included the first-token time in the rate. A word is not a token, and TTFT is not decode time. Use the benchmark client, which counts tokens and keeps TTFT and TPOT apart.

### The rules

1. One client, one version, named in every result.
2. One temperature, named in every result.
3. `--random-range-ratio 1.0`, or the length distribution written down.
4. A flush and a new seed before every run, and the cached tokens recorded.
5. The GPU clock recorded and the hot runs set aside.
6. Throughput reported only together with the median and P99 TTFT and TPOT at the same cap.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why does the default range ratio describe half the work? Expected: each length is drawn from 1 to the length asked, so the average prompt is about half of it; with 1.0 every prompt has the full length and the input token total in the report confirms it.
- **Level 3:** Fixed lengths gave a late first token and a steady stream, mixed lengths the opposite. Which do you use? Expected: fixed lengths to compare two builds, because they repeat exactly; your real length mix before you set a latency target, because the two shapes measure two different servers.
- **Level 3:** A teammate's hand-written timing loop reads 13 tokens per second where a hosted API reads 60. What is wrong with the loop? Expected: it counted words split on spaces and included the first-token time in the rate; a word is not a token and TTFT is not decode time, so use the benchmark client.
- **Level 4:** At 16 requests per second the client reports a first token you do not believe. How do you check the client itself? Expected: a single-process client adds its own queue at high rates; run two client processes that each send half the rate and compare, and record the CPU use of the client.

## Wrong answers

- "Both are standard clients, so the numbers are comparable." On one server the SGLang client read 3 to 10 percent higher first-token times and 2 to 8 percent lower throughput than the vLLM client; a gap of a few percent can come from the client alone.
- "Temperature does not change speed." Temperature 0.7 raised the median time per token 10 to 13 percent at one user and 3 to 6 percent at 16 and 64 users over temperature 0.
- "Set the input length to 512 and the prompts are 512 tokens." With the default range ratio of 0.0 the average prompt is about 256 tokens; pass 1.0 or state the distribution.
- "A load tester that handles HTTP handles model traffic." A generic tool sends one prompt in a loop, which hits the prefix cache almost every time, and it does not read the token gaps of a stream; use a client that samples prompt lengths and counts tokens.

## Taught in

[Benchmark your server in 15 minutes](../../../manuals/vllm-101/sections/5-1-benchmark-your-server-in-15-minutes.md) and [the SGLang benchmark section](../../../manuals/sglang-101/sections/5-1-sglang-benchmark-serving.md) compare the clients, and [the load testing lesson](../../../phases/17-infrastructure-and-production/22-load-testing-llm-apis/docs/en.md) names the two client traps.

interviews.title: What determinism costs a live server
interviews.markdown:
Your evaluation team wants bit-identical outputs from the live server and asks you to enable batch invariance for all traffic. What does it change, what does it cost, and what would you say?

## Short answer

The mode replaces the kernels that split their sums by the batch size with kernels that keep one reduction order, so one request gives the same logits alone and in a batch. It costs speed, most at low concurrency: on our L4 the small model paid 2.4 times the time per token at one user and 1.4 times at 32, and Qwen3-8B paid 1.4 times at 8 users with 27 percent less output. I would turn it on for evaluation and rollout servers and leave it off for production traffic, after I measured the cost at the concurrency we serve, because on SGLang with the default backend it also turns prefix caching off.

## Full answer

### What the mode switches

On vLLM, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` needs a GPU of compute capability 8.0 or higher, which includes the L4 and the GB10, and it turns off speed features that change the order of the sums, such as custom all-reduce with tensor parallelism. At 0.31.0 it is in beta.

On SGLang, `--enable-deterministic-inference` replaces the matrix multiply, the log-softmax, the mean, the RMS norm and the batched multiply with batch-invariant kernels, forces the plain sampling backend, sets the all-reduce to a tree so that tensor-parallel sums add in a fixed order, accepts only some attention backends, turns the radix cache off unless the backend is one that supports it, and gives every request without a `sampling_seed` the seed 42. The cache rule matters most: with the default backend on the GB10 the log said that the radix cache is not compatible, so every repeated prefix paid its full prefill again. On the L4 the mode picked a different backend that keeps the cache on.

### What the manual measured

vLLM on the L4 with the clock locked at 900 MHz, Qwen3-0.6B, runs in the order default, batch-invariant, default again, two seeds each with a cache reset before each run:

| Users | Median TPOT, default / batch-invariant | Output tok/s, default / batch-invariant |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6.9 / 16.9 ms (2.4x) | 140.6 / 58.7 (58% lower) |
| 8 | 9.9 / 18.2 ms (1.8x) | 755 / 420 (44% lower) |
| 32 | 18.8 / 25.9 ms (1.4x) | 1,565 / 1,154 (26% lower) |

On Qwen3-8B at 8 users the time per token was 1.4 times longer and the output 27 percent lower; at 32 users 1.3 times and 23 percent. The relative cost fell as more users shared each step, and it was larger on the small model.

SGLang on the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B, one run per server at concurrency 8: output fell from 78.92 to 64.83 tokens per second, 18 percent, and the median time per token rose from 97.30 to 117.43 ms. The radix cache was off in that run, so a workload with shared prefixes pays more than this number shows.

### What other teams measured

A post on nondeterminism ran 1,000 Qwen3-8B requests on vLLM in 26 s by default, 55 s with batch-invariant kernels, and 42 s with a better attention kernel. A 2026 study measured batch-invariant kernels at more than twice the latency and up to 74 percent less throughput. A verification study found that the modes of both engines gave different logits under some changes in execution, such as prompt chunking and KV cache reuse. The manual did not measure these itself.

### What the mode does not cover

At 0.31.0 a vLLM model that picks its own attention backend skips the check, so its output can still depend on the batch; the next release checks every attention layer, and a fix for expert models with data, tensor and expert parallelism under compile is not in it. On SGLang a hybrid state-space model was reported as not batch-invariant, some newer architectures are not yet supported, a sliding-window kernel gave several greedy outputs in prefix mode with the issue still open, and one speculative algorithm gave different text after a restart because kernel autotuning picked different tactics on each start.

### What I would say

Use the mode where identical bits are the product: reinforcement learning rollouts and evaluations that must reproduce. Keep production traffic on the default kernels, where prefix caching and faster kernels are worth more than identical bits. Measure the cost at the concurrency you serve, not at one point, and test the exact setup: model, attention backend, parallel layout, chunk size and cache setting. Flush the cache between two runs you compare, and keep the dtype the same.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why did the relative cost shrink at higher concurrency? Expected: the invariant kernels give up the fast splits that an idle GPU would use, and that loss is a larger share of a small step; with more rows per step the fixed order costs a smaller share, 1.4 times at 32 users against 2.4 at one.
- **Level 3:** On SGLang the 18 percent understates the cost for a chat workload. Why? Expected: with the default attention backend deterministic mode turns the radix cache off, so every repeated prefix pays its full prefill again; pick a backend that keeps the cache where the GPU supports it.
- **Level 4:** Two servers both run the mode and still give different greedy text for one prompt. Name three causes. Expected: different hardware or engine version; a model path the mode does not cover, such as an attention layer that picks its own backend or a hybrid state-space layer; and kernel autotuning that picked different tactics on each start.

## Wrong answers

- "The mode has no cost when the GPU is idle." The cost is largest at low concurrency, 2.4 times the time per token at one user on the small model, because the invariant kernels give up the fast splits that an idle GPU would use.
- "Turn it on for production, because correctness comes first." Production traffic gains more from prefix caching and fast kernels than from identical bits; the manual's position is to use the mode for rollouts and evaluations and to measure the cost at the concurrency you serve.
- "The flag covers every model." At 0.31.0 a model that picks its own attention backend skips the check, hybrid state-space layers are not covered, and a fix for expert models under compile is not in the next release; test the exact setup.
- "The seed 42 makes sampled requests reproducible." It makes every request without a sampling_seed draw the same random numbers, which is reproducible and also identical across users; set a sampling_seed per request that must reproduce.

## Taught in

[Get reproducible outputs](../../../manuals/vllm-101/sections/3-8-get-reproducible-outputs.md) measures the cost on the L4, and [the SGLang deterministic inference section](../../../manuals/sglang-101/sections/4-6-deterministic-inference-and-logprobs.md) lists what the flag switches.

interviews.title: A larger token budget at low load
interviews.markdown:
A teammate proposes `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384` so that long prompts get their first token sooner. The server runs a model with mixture-of-experts layers on one card. Requests arrive at about half a request per second, with prompts between 1,024 and 4,096 tokens. What do you expect to change, and what would you measure before you accept the change?

## Short answer

A larger budget lets a long prompt finish its prefill in fewer steps, but each of those steps takes longer, and every running stream waits for it. At low load I expect a faster first token and a worse P99 ITL, and I would measure both with several seeds at the real request rate. On our GB10 at 0.5 requests per second, 16,384 raised the P99 ITL from 574 to 798 ms, while the first-token gain did not clear the seed spread.

## Full answer

### What the manual measured

Budgets of 2,048 and 16,384 tokens on the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B, requests at a fixed rate, three seeds per point, each request asking for 64 to 256 tokens:

| Requests per second | Budget | Median TTFT | Median TPOT | P99 ITL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 2,048 | 1,145 ms | 149.3 ms | 574 ms |
| 0.5 | 16,384 | 906 ms | 139.4 ms | 798 ms |
| 1 | 2,048 | 454 ms | 156.5 ms | 405 ms |
| 1 | 16,384 | 477 ms | 156.9 ms | 395 ms |
| 2 | 2,048 | 560 ms | 205.5 ms | 587 ms |
| 2 | 16,384 | 595 ms | 205.1 ms | 586 ms |

At 0.5 requests per second the larger budget raised the P99 ITL by 39 percent, and the seed ranges did not overlap. The first token came sooner, but the seed ranges of the first token overlapped. So the cost is clear and the gain is not confirmed. At 1 and 2 requests per second the two budgets gave the same numbers within the seed ranges. All runs held a median clock of 2,398 to 2,411 MHz, so the clock does not explain any row.

### Why the effect fades with the rate

At a higher rate more requests share each step. One long prompt then fills a smaller share of the budget, and how it is chunked matters less. The result is narrow: two budgets, three low rates, one model, one machine. The P-PAS paper found that no single fixed budget was best at every load: a large budget won at low prefill pressure, a small one when several prefills competed with running streams.

### An open result

The median first token at 0.5 requests per second was slower than at 1 request per second for both budgets. All three seeds at 0.5 were above 900 ms with the 2,048 budget, and all three at 1 were below 600 ms. One slow seed does not explain it. The manual did not find the cause and says so.

### How to decide

1. Read the budget that your server uses. The run with no flag matched 2,048 on this machine.
2. If the P99 ITL is too high and long prompts arrive, lower the budget.
3. If the first token of long prompts is too slow and the P99 ITL has room, raise it.
4. Measure at your real request rate, and again when your load changes.

`--long-prefill-token-threshold` caps the tokens that one long prompt gets in a step when other requests wait. It is off by default and the manual did not test it.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** At the two higher rates the budgets tied. Why does the difference vanish as the rate rises? Expected: more requests share each step, so one long prompt fills a smaller share of the budget and its chunking matters less.
- **Level 3:** Both budgets gave a later first token at the lowest rate than at the next rate up. How do you report that? Expected: all three seeds agreed, so it is not one slow seed; the cause was not found, so it stays an open result and no rule is built on it.
- **Level 4:** Is there one budget that wins at every load? Expected: no; a large budget wins when prefill pressure is low and a small one when several prefills compete with streams, so the value must move with the load.

## Wrong answers

- "A larger budget is free because the GPU has spare compute at low load." Each step with a bigger chunk takes longer and every running stream waits for it; the P99 ITL rose 39 percent at 0.5 requests per second.
- "Set the budget once from the GPU size and leave it." The best value moved with the request rate in these runs, so measure at your real rate and again when the load changes.
- "The drop from 1,145 to 906 ms proves the first-token gain." The seed ranges of the first token overlapped, so the cost is confirmed and the gain is not.

## Taught in

[Keep long prompts from stalling short ones](../../../manuals/vllm-101/sections/3-3-keep-long-prompts-from-stalling-short-ones.md) has the six measured rows and the tuning order.

interviews.title: Two data-parallel copies, less output than one card
interviews.markdown:
You add a second L4 to an SGLang server with `--dp-size 2` and expect about twice the throughput. The sweep shows less than one card gave: at 64 users the pair peaks at 64 tokens per second and falls to 42, and the P99 first token is 391 seconds against 33.4 on one card. Both copies loaded the weights without an error. What do you check, and what went wrong?

## Short answer

Read the `KV Cache is allocated` line of every DP rank before you trust the sum. On that pair the second card ran two pods of another team, so its copy had 3.17 GB free after the weights against 6.59 GB and a pool of 2,925 tokens against 24,094, an eighth of the first. The round-robin controller does not look at pools, so it sent every second request to the small copy, where 4 ran and 59 waited, while the large copy held one to three requests and used 2 to 7 percent of its pool.

## Full answer

### The two pools

The startup lines of the two ranks tell the story before the first request:

- `DP0` loaded the weights in 3.61 s and had 6.59 GB left; its pool was 24,094 tokens.
- `DP1` loaded the same 15.28 GB of weights in 3.73 s and had 3.17 GB left, because two pods of 1,746 MiB each held the rest; its pool was 2,925 tokens. Four requests of 640 tokens fill it.

The decode lines at 64 running requests show the result. `DP1` ran 4 requests at a token usage of 0.82 to 0.87 with 59 in its queue. `DP0` ran one to three requests at a usage of 0.02 to 0.07 with an empty queue.

### Why the client could not help

The benchmark keeps 64 requests open at a time. Round robin alternates requests between the copies without a look at pools or queues. At 64 users, 63 requests sat on the small copy, 4 running and 59 waiting. The client could not send the large copy more work until the small copy gave a slot back.

### What it cost

One L4 reached 270 tokens per second. The pair peaked at 64 and fell to 42 as its clock fell: it ran at 765 and 675 MHz at 32 and 64 users, under the manual's clock floor, while the single card ran at 1,320 and 1,080 MHz, so part of the loss is the clock. At 64 users the median P99 first token of three seeds was 33.4 seconds on one card and 391 seconds on the pair. Up to 4 users the pair was already 16 to 41 percent slower for a reason the manual did not isolate, and at one user it took 79.6 ms per token against 60.2 at a higher clock. With a fixed arrival rate the pair completed at most 0.21 requests per second inside the latency target, against 0.96 for one card.

### Route by tokens

`--load-balance-method total_tokens` sends each request to the copy that holds the fewest tokens. On the same uneven pair it gave 114.7 tokens per second at 64 users, against 41.7 with round robin and 250.9 on one L4. At 8 users it gave 92.1 against 64.2 and 112.6. The median first token at 64 users fell from 4,763 to 3,977 ms. That run had a median clock of 1,020 MHz against 675 in the round-robin run, so part of the gain is the card. A large gain over round robin, and still a loss against one card.

### Tensor parallelism would have refused

`--tp-size 2` on the same pair stopped two seconds after the collective library started. Before it loads weights, each rank measures its free memory and the group keeps the smallest value. If that value is under 90 percent of the local free memory, the server stops. The shared card had 18.28 GB free against the 19.53 GB that the check required. Each rank of a tensor group holds the same share of weights and the same pool, so the smallest card sets the size for all. `--dp-size 2` has no such check, because each copy sizes its own pool, so it started and lost.

### The rule

Add capacity with copies only when every copy has about the same pool. Give a group whole GPUs on a shared machine. Check the `#tokens` line of each DP rank before you count on the sum. The other fix, two separate servers behind a gateway with weights, the manual did not measure.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why did the large copy sit almost idle while 59 requests waited? Expected: the benchmark is a closed loop with 64 open requests, round robin put half of them on the small copy, and the client could not send new work to the large copy until the small copy returned a slot.
- **Level 3:** Why did a tensor split refuse the same pair while the data-parallel pair started? Expected: tensor parallelism checks that every rank has at least 90 percent of the local free memory, because every rank holds the same share and pool, and the shared card had 18.28 GB against the 19.53 GB required; data parallelism sizes each copy's pool on its own and has no such check.
- **Level 4:** Routing by total tokens lifted the pair to 114.7 at 64 users. Is the problem solved? Expected: no; one card alone gave 250.9, the token-routed run also had a higher clock than the round-robin run so part of the gain is the card, and the fix is equal pools, with whole GPUs for each copy or separate servers behind a gateway with weights.

## Wrong answers

- "Both copies loaded, so the second card is fine." The weights need 15.28 GB on each card; the pool is sized from what is left, and the shared card had 3.17 GB left against 6.59, an eighth of the pool.
- "The controller balances load, so a slow copy gets fewer requests." The default round robin does not look at pools or queues; it alternated requests, so 63 of 64 open requests ended on the small copy.
- "The pair is slower because of the clock, so run it again when the card is cool." The pair did run under the clock floor at 32 and 64 users, but it was already 16 to 41 percent slower up to 4 users, and the log shows 59 requests waiting on one copy; the pool explains the shape and the clock explains part of the size.

## Taught in

[The SGLang parallelism section](../../../manuals/sglang-101/sections/6-1-tp-size-dp-size-and-attn-dp-size.md) has the two-pool listing, the sweep and the routing fix.

interviews.title: When prefill-decode disaggregation pays
interviews.markdown:
Your chat users see a smooth stream until someone pastes a long document, and then every stream pauses while the server prefills it. A colleague proposes prefill-decode disaggregation: separate prefill servers and decode servers. When does that split pay, what does it not do, and how would you decide?

## Short answer

Split prefill from decode when the measured problem is the tail of the inter-token latency and long prompts cause it, because a prefill server then never shares a step with a stream. It does not raise throughput: the documentation says so, it costs a KV transfer for every request plus more servers and a router, and a 2025 study found that even the tail gain depends on the load and on the path that moves the cache. Decide with a measurement: one server first, then copies behind a gateway, and the split last, compared with the same GPUs run as plain servers at your real load.

## Full answer

### What it solves and what it does not

On one server a long prompt shares each step with the running streams, and every stream waits a little longer for its next token. Chunked prefill makes the pause shorter but cannot remove it. Two kinds of server remove it: a prefill server computes the prompt and builds its KV cache, and a decode server receives that cache and writes the answer.

The vLLM documentation says that disaggregated prefill does not raise throughput. It gives control over the first token and the stream as two separate numbers, and it controls the tail of the inter-token latency. Even that gain is a condition, not a default: the study that compared split servers with servers that run both stages found that it depends on the request load and on the path that moves the cache.

### How the cache moves

In SGLang the gateway starts every exchange. It picks one prefill server and one decode server, adds the bootstrap host and port of the prefill server and a random 63-bit room number, and sends the same request to both. The decode server reserves KV slots and publishes their addresses. The prefill server runs a normal prefill and writes the KV pages straight into those slots, a one-sided RDMA write with the default transfer backend, or over TCP on a cluster without RDMA cards. The decode server sees the transfer finish and adds the request to its running batch. Every transfer moves through bootstrapping, waiting, transferring and success, and any stage can fail. The bootstrap port defaults to 8998, both timeouts to 300 seconds, and the transfer queue count to 4.

In vLLM each server gets a KV connector and a role, `kv_producer` or `kv_consumer`, and the common connector needs a library that the wheel does not install, pinned at 1.4.1. A router sends each request to the prefill server first, reads the transfer parameters from its response, and sends the request to the decode server with them. If a transfer fails, the default policy fails the request; `kv_load_failure_policy` set to `recompute` computes the prompt again on the decode server instead.

Never send a request straight to a role server. The scheduler asserts that a bootstrap room exists and tells you to use the router.

### The order to decide

1. Measure TTFT and inter-token latency on one server with a benchmark that mixes long and short prompts.
2. Add data-parallel copies behind a gateway, and measure again.
3. Split only when the inter-token tail still rises when long prompts arrive, and compare the split with the same GPUs as plain servers at your real load.

### Size the two sides

Long prompts with short answers need more prefill capacity. Short prompts with long answers need more decode capacity. One test on eight GPUs found that at high concurrency one prefill server for three decode servers won every metric, while at low concurrency three to one and two to two gave a better first token. It shows the direction, not your ratio. Measure the first token and the stream on each side and move one server at a time.

### What went wrong for other teams

- A pair with one prefill and one decode server had a higher first token than one plain server with the same split of GPUs. An old transfer library was the cause, and an upgrade fixed it. Without the single-server baseline nobody would have known.
- At 64 concurrent requests one setup logged many bootstrap failures and `Aborted by AbortReq` on the prefill side, while 4 to 7 concurrent requests worked. The router's timeout for the prefill client was too short, and a later fix lengthened it. The rule: an abort means the client or the router aborted, so check timeouts before you suspect the transfer.
- With the overlap scheduler on, one deployment saw throughput rise about 10 percent and the first token get much worse, because the KV transfer waited for the next kernel launch; their fix was a flag that the manual could not find in the pinned version.

### What to watch after the split

The bootstrap-failed and transfer-failed counters must stay flat. The transfer latency and speed gauges show the cost of each move. The decode pre-allocation and transfer queue gauges show requests that wait for memory or for a transfer. In every benchmark, read the retokenized output tokens before the throughput.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** On the same GPUs, the split pair's first token arrives later than the plain server's. What do you suspect first? Expected: the transfer path, an old transfer library or a router timeout; one incident fixed it with an upgrade, and only the single-server baseline showed that the split made it worse.
- **Level 3:** Prefill logs aborts at a load of 64 users and works at 4 to 7. Where is the fault? Expected: in the router or client timeouts, which aborted requests that were still running, not in the transfer; a later fix lengthened the router timeout.
- **Level 4:** How do you pick the ratio of prefill to decode servers? Expected: from your prompt and answer lengths and your concurrency; long prompts with short answers need more prefill and the reverse more decode; one test found one prefill for three decode servers won at high concurrency and three to one or two to two gave a better first token at low concurrency, so measure both sides and move one server at a time.

## Wrong answers

- "Disaggregation raises throughput." The documentation says it does not; it gives control over the first token and the stream as two numbers and costs a KV transfer per request and more servers.
- "Send requests straight to the decode server to skip the router." The scheduler asserts that a bootstrap room exists and tells you to send requests to the router; the room is how the two servers find each other's half of one request.
- "A failed transfer falls back to a normal prefill." The vLLM default policy fails the request; set the failure policy to recompute if you want the decode server to compute the prompt again.
- "Chunked prefill already solves this." It makes the pause shorter but cannot remove it, because the chunk still shares the step with the running decodes; the split removes the sharing at the cost of a transfer and a second set of failures.

## Taught in

[Split prefill and decode](../../../manuals/vllm-101/sections/6-3-split-prefill-and-decode.md) and [the SGLang disaggregation section](../../../manuals/sglang-101/sections/6-3-prefill-decode-disaggregation.md) cover the setup, the limits and the incidents.

interviews.title: Bag the deep trees or boost the stumps
interviews.markdown:
You have a tabular dataset and two candidate base learners: deep decision trees that fit the training rows almost perfectly, and decision stumps that barely beat a constant. You can afford one ensemble method for each. Which one gets bagging and which one gets boosting, and why?

## Short answer

Bag the deep trees and boost the stumps. Deep trees have low bias and high variance, and averaging many of them trained on bootstrap samples cancels the variance without adding bias. Stumps have high bias and low variance, and boosting builds them in sequence so each new one corrects the errors of the ensemble so far, which drives the bias down.

## Full answer

### Match the method to the error term

Expected error splits into squared bias, variance and irreducible noise. The two methods attack different terms.

| Method | Reduces | Bias | Variance | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bagging, random forest | variance | no change | decreases | does nothing for bias |
| Boosting | bias | decreases | can increase | overfits with too many rounds |

### Why bagging fits the deep trees

Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample, a draw with replacement of the same size as the data, which holds about 63.2 percent of the unique rows. The rest, about 36.8 percent, are out-of-bag and give a free validation set. The average of N independent predictions with variance sigma squared has variance sigma squared over N. The trees are not independent, because they see similar data, so the gain is smaller than that, and a random forest adds a random feature subset at each split, square root of the feature count for classification, to make the trees disagree more. Adding trees lowers variance and never adds bias, so test accuracy plateaus and does not fall.

### Why boosting fits the stumps

Boosting trains learners in sequence. AdaBoost raises the weight of rows the ensemble gets wrong, so the next stump works on them. Gradient boosting fits each new tree to the negative gradient of the loss, which for squared error is the residual. Each round removes some of the systematic error, which is the bias. The learning rate scales each tree's contribution; the lesson gives 0.01 to 0.3, and a smaller value needs more trees and generalizes better. Because later rounds chase the hardest rows, boosting can fit noise, so it needs early stopping on a validation loss.

### Why not the other way round

Boosting the deep trees has little bias left to remove and stacks high variance learners, so it overfits fast. Bagging the stumps averages many models that all miss the same pattern, so the average misses it too. Diversity is the requirement in both cases: the lesson's majority vote of 21 independent classifiers at 60 percent accuracy reaches about 74 percent, and 101 of them reach about 84 percent, only because their errors differ.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why does bagging the deep trees not fix bias? Expected: the average of many models that miss the same pattern misses it too; averaging only removes their disagreement.
- **Level 3:** What does the learning rate do in gradient boosting? Expected: it scales each tree's contribution; a smaller rate needs more trees and generalizes better.
- **Level 4:** Boosting's training error keeps falling while validation error rises. What happened and what do you do? Expected: later rounds fit noisy or mislabeled rows; stop early on the validation loss, or lower the learning rate and the tree depth.
- **Level 4:** Why does a forest's test accuracy plateau but not fall as trees are added? Expected: each tree lowers variance and none adds bias, so more trees cannot overfit the way more boosting rounds can.

## Wrong answers

- "Boost the deep trees, since boosting is the stronger method." A low bias, high variance learner has little bias to remove, and boosting amplifies its variance.
- "Bag the stumps to make them strong." Averaging stumps that all underfit still underfits; bagging leaves bias where it is.
- "Any ensemble of enough models beats a single one." Gains need diverse errors; models that make the same mistakes do not cancel them.

## Taught in

The [ensemble methods lesson](../../../phases/02-ml-fundamentals/11-ensemble-methods/) builds both methods, the [bias-variance lesson](../../../phases/02-ml-fundamentals/10-bias-variance/) gives the rule for which to use, and the [decision trees lesson](../../../phases/02-ml-fundamentals/04-decision-trees/) builds the forest.

interviews.title: Pick a 16-bit format for training and one for inference
interviews.markdown:
Your training stack can run in float16 or in bfloat16. A teammate picks float16 because it keeps more digits. Which format do you pick for training, which for inference, and what extra mechanism does one of them need?

## Short answer

Pick bfloat16 for training. It has the same 8-bit exponent as float32, so it covers the same range up to about 3.4e38, and activations, logits and gradients that spike past 65,504 do not overflow. float16 has 10 mantissa bits and more precision, but its 5-bit exponent caps at 65,504 and underflows gradients below about 6e-8, so it needs loss scaling to train. For inference, where values are bounded and precision matters more, float16 is the usual choice.

## Full answer

### The two layouts

```text
float16:   [1 sign] [5 exponent]  [10 mantissa]   max about 65,504
bfloat16:  [1 sign] [8 exponent]  [7 mantissa]    max about 3.4e38
```

The mantissa sets precision, the exponent sets range. Training needs range: a loss spike, a large logit or a tiny gradient all live far from 1. Inference values are bounded by the trained weights, so the extra three mantissa bits of float16 are worth more there.

### What goes wrong in float16

- Overflow: an activation above 65,504 becomes inf, and inf poisons every value downstream.
- Underflow: gradients are often around 1e-8 or smaller, and float16 rounds anything below about 6e-8 to zero. The weights stop moving, with no error.

### Loss scaling

Mixed precision keeps a float32 master copy of the weights, runs the forward and backward passes in the 16-bit format, and computes the loss in float32. To keep float16 gradients above the underflow floor, multiply the loss by a large constant such as 1024 before backward, so every gradient is 1024 times larger, then divide the gradients by the same constant before the update. The update is unchanged. Dynamic loss scaling starts high, at 65536 in the lesson, halves the scale on the first inf gradient, and doubles it again after a run of clean steps.

### Why bfloat16 skips most of this

bfloat16 is the top 16 bits of a float32: drop the low mantissa bits and the exponent is unchanged. Its range covers the gradient spectrum, so loss scaling is usually unnecessary, and conversion is a truncation. The cost is precision: about 2 to 3 decimal digits, against 3 to 4 for float16.

### Symptoms that point here

The lesson's bug list has three entries with this cause: validation accuracy 1 to 3 percent below the paper after a switch to float16, gradient norms of 0.0 in some layers, and a run that diverges after moving from float32 to float16. The fixes are loss scaling or bfloat16.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why do small gradients vanish in float16 and not in bfloat16? Expected: float16's smallest normal values sit near 6e-8 and smaller gradients round to 0; bfloat16's exponent reaches float32's range.
- **Level 3:** What does dynamic loss scaling do when a gradient turns inf? Expected: skip the step, halve the scale, and double it again after a run of clean steps.
- **Level 4:** You moved from float32 to float16 and validation accuracy fell by a few percent with no error. What happened? Expected: gradient underflow zeroed small updates; enable loss scaling or move to bfloat16.
- **Level 4:** Why is bfloat16 cheap to convert from float32? Expected: it is the top 16 bits of a float32, so conversion drops the low mantissa bits and the exponent is unchanged.

## Wrong answers

- "More mantissa bits means better training, so float16 wins." Training is limited by range; a logit spike past 65,504 becomes inf in float16 and is fine in bfloat16.
- "Loss scaling changes the training result." Dividing the gradients by the same factor before the update gives the same update; the scale only lifts small values above the underflow floor.
- "Use bfloat16 everywhere, inference included." Inference values are bounded and the extra float16 precision helps there; the lesson makes float16 the inference default.

## Taught in

The [numerical stability lesson](../../../phases/01-math-foundations/13-numerical-stability/) compares the formats, explains loss scaling, and lists the mixed precision bugs.

interviews.title: Decide whether a small win on one split is real
interviews.markdown:
Two variants of a classifier differ by one hyperparameter. On one held-out split, variant B beats variant A by a small margin, and the team wants to ship B. Design the evaluation that decides whether B is better, and say what you would report.

## Short answer

One split gives one noisy number, so the gap could be chance. Run k-fold cross-validation with the same folds for both variants, keep the per-fold differences, and test whether their mean is far from zero with a paired t-statistic. Report the mean and spread of each variant's fold scores, the mean difference and the statistic, and keep the test set out of the comparison.

## Full answer

### Why one split is not enough

A single split depends on which rows landed in each part. A different seed gives a different gap, and nothing in one number says how large that swing is. Folds show the spread.

### The design

1. Hold the test set out before anything else. It is for the final report, once.
2. Build K folds on the training data. The lesson uses K equal to 5 and names 5 or 10 as the standard choices. Stratify when the classes are imbalanced, so every fold keeps the class ratio.
3. Train and score both variants on the same folds, so the two scores in each fold are a pair. Pairing removes the fold-to-fold variation from the difference.
4. Compute the per-fold differences, their mean and their standard deviation, and the paired t-statistic: mean difference divided by the standard deviation over the square root of K. The lesson's threshold for 5 folds is a t-statistic whose magnitude exceeds 2.78, for significance at p below 0.05 with 4 degrees of freedom.
5. If the hyperparameter was chosen on these folds, wrap the whole thing in nested cross-validation: an inner loop picks the value, an outer loop measures it.
6. Repeat with a few fold seeds and check the conclusion holds.

### What to report

- Each variant's mean fold score with its spread.
- The mean difference, the statistic and the fold count.
- The effect size in product terms, so the team can weigh it against the cost of the change.
- One test set number for the variant you ship, measured once at the end.

### Caveats to say out loud

The folds share training rows, so the t-test is an approximation, not a clean independent sample. A significant difference can still be too small to matter. And a comparison made on the test set turns it into a validation set, which is the mistake the design is built to prevent.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why must both variants use the same folds? Expected: pairing removes the fold-to-fold variation from the difference, so the test asks only about the variants.
- **Level 4:** What does an absolute t above 2.78 mean with five folds? Expected: with 4 degrees of freedom the mean difference is unlikely to be zero at the 5 percent level, so the gap is probably real.
- **Level 4:** How do you avoid tuning on the folds you report? Expected: nested cross-validation; the inner loop picks the hyperparameter and the outer loop measures it, so the reported folds never saw the choice.
- **Level 4:** The difference is significant and tiny. Do you ship B? Expected: weigh the effect size against the cost of the change; significance says the sign is reliable, not that it matters.

## Wrong answers

- "One held-out split is enough if it is large." A single split still depends on which rows landed where; folds show the spread.
- "Compare the two mean scores and pick the higher one." Without the per-fold pairing and the spread, a gap smaller than the fold noise looks like a win.
- "Use the test set to break the tie." The test set is single use; a choice made on it turns it into a validation set.

## Taught in

The [model evaluation lesson](../../../phases/02-ml-fundamentals/09-model-evaluation/) builds k-fold and stratified k-fold from scratch and ends with a paired comparison of two models.

interviews.title: Why minimizing cross-entropy also minimizes KL
interviews.markdown:
Your classifier trains on a cross-entropy loss. A reviewer asks why you do not train on the KL divergence between the labels and the predictions instead. Explain how the two quantities relate and what would change, if anything, in training.

## Short answer

Cross-entropy of P and Q equals the entropy of P plus the KL divergence from P to Q. The labels fix P, so their entropy is a constant during training, and the two objectives have the same gradient. With one-hot labels the entropy is zero and the two numbers are equal: minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class.

## Full answer

### The three quantities

```text
H(P)     = - sum_x p(x) log p(x)             entropy of the true distribution
H(P, Q)  = - sum_x p(x) log q(x)             cross-entropy, P true, Q predicted
KL(P||Q) =   sum_x p(x) log (p(x) / q(x))    = H(P, Q) - H(P)
```

Entropy is the average surprise of P under its own code. Cross-entropy is the average surprise when events from P are coded with Q. KL is the extra surprise, the bits wasted by coding with Q instead of P.

### Why the optimizer cannot tell them apart

The model controls Q. The labels fix P, so H(P) is a constant for each sample. The gradient of a constant is zero, so the gradient of H(P, Q) and the gradient of KL(P||Q) with respect to the model are the same. With a one-hot label the sum has one nonzero term, H(P) is 0, and the loss is minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class.

### When the two numbers differ

The values differ when the target has positive entropy. Label smoothing turns a hard target into a soft one, and a teacher's softmax in distillation is soft from the start. Then cross-entropy cannot go below H(P), while KL reaches 0 at a perfect match. The gradients are still equal, so the choice changes the number you log, not the model you get.

### Two facts to say out loud

- KL is not symmetric. KL(P||Q) and KL(Q||P) weight the log ratio by different distributions, so it is not a distance.
- The gradient of cross-entropy with respect to the logits is the predicted probability minus the target. That clean form is why it pairs with softmax.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why is KL not a distance? Expected: it is not symmetric; each direction weights the log ratio by a different distribution.
- **Level 3:** With label smoothing the loss never reaches zero. Why? Expected: the soft target has positive entropy, and cross-entropy is at least the entropy of the target; KL would reach zero at a perfect match.
- **Level 3:** Differentiate the loss by each logit. What form do you get? Expected: the predicted probability minus the target, for each class.
- **Level 4:** In distillation the target is a teacher's softmax. Which of the two numbers do you log? Expected: KL, because the teacher's entropy is a constant offset per sample that hides how close the student is; the gradient is the same either way.

## Wrong answers

- "They are different objectives and give different models." They differ by the entropy of the labels, which does not depend on the model, so the gradients are equal.
- "Cross-entropy is a distance between two distributions." It is not symmetric, and it is not zero when the distributions match; it equals the entropy of P at a match.
- "KL is smaller, so it is the better loss." KL is cross-entropy minus a constant. The optimizer sees the same slope.

## Taught in

The [information theory lesson](../../../phases/01-math-foundations/09-information-theory/) derives entropy, cross-entropy and KL from scratch and shows the three views of the classification loss.

interviews.title: Read a shape error in a dense layer
interviews.markdown:
A colleague builds a dense layer that takes 784 inputs and gives 128 outputs. The first forward pass stops with a shape error. Which dimensions does the weight matrix need, and how do you read an error like this one?

## Short answer

The matrix is 128 by 784: one row for each output and one column for each input. A matrix product needs the inner sizes to agree, so a 128 by 784 matrix times a 784 by 1 input gives a 128 by 1 output. An error means the inner sizes differ, and the fix starts with the shapes of every operand written on paper.

## Full answer

### The rule

A product of an m by n matrix and an n by p matrix gives an m by p matrix. The inner sizes, both n, must agree. For the layer in the question:

```text
(128 x 784) @ (784 x 1) = (128 x 1)
  weights       input       output
```

The rows of the weight matrix count the outputs. The columns count the inputs. Each output is the dot product of one weight row with the whole input vector.

### The bias

The bias holds one value for each output. Store it as a 128 by 1 column, as the lesson does, so that it adds to the 128 by 1 result element by element. A flat array of 128 values against a 128 by 1 column broadcasts to 128 by 128 with no error. When the layer runs on a batch, the bias has fewer dimensions than the output, and broadcasting repeats it across the batch. Broadcasting only stretches a dimension of size 1, so it never fixes a 784 against a 128.

### How to read the error

1. Write the shape of every operand next to the operation.
2. Find the operation whose inner sizes do not match. That is the broken line.
3. Decide which side is wrong. A transposed weight matrix, an input stored as a row instead of a column, and a missing batch dimension each give a different pair of numbers in the message.

The lesson makes the same check for a two layer network: the first matrix is 4 by 3 and the second is 2 by 4, so a 3 by 1 input gives a 4 by 1 hidden vector and a 2 by 1 output.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 1:** What shape does the bias have? Expected: one value for each output, so 128 values, stored as a 128 by 1 column so that it adds to each output column.
- **Level 2:** A batch of inputs arrives as rows instead of columns. What changes? Expected: the order of the product changes, so the batch matrix times the transposed weight gives one output row for each input.
- **Level 2:** Why does a transpose appear in the backward pass? Expected: the gradient for the input needs the weight matrix with its rows and columns swapped, so that the shapes agree in the reverse direction.
- **Level 3:** How does broadcasting hide a shape bug? Expected: a dimension of size 1 is stretched to fit, so a wrong shape can run without an error and give wrong values. An assertion on the shape catches it.

## Wrong answers

- "The weight matrix is 784 by 128 because inputs come first." With a column input the matrix needs 128 rows and 784 columns. The order of the product decides which form is right, not the order in which you name the sizes.
- "Shapes do not matter, the framework fixes them." Broadcasting repeats only a dimension of size 1. A 784 against a 128 inner size is an error, or a silent wrong result after a reshape.
- "Transpose things until the code runs." A transpose that makes the code run can multiply the wrong pairs of numbers. Write the shapes down first and then change the one that is wrong.

## Taught in

The [vectors and matrices lesson](../../../phases/01-math-foundations/02-vectors-matrices-operations/) gives the shape rule and builds a dense layer from a Matrix class.

interviews.title: Two products in NumPy that print different numbers
interviews.markdown:
Read this code and say what each print shows. Then tell me which of the two operations a dense layer uses, and why.

```python
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
print(A * B)
print(A @ B)
```

## Short answer

The star multiplies matching positions, so the first print shows 5, 12, 21 and 32. The at sign forms dot products of rows with columns, so the second print shows 19, 22, 43 and 50. A layer uses the at sign, because every output must sum over every input.

## Full answer

### Element-wise product

Both arrays have the same shape, so the star pairs each cell with the cell at the same position:

```text
1*5 = 5    2*6 = 12
3*7 = 21   4*8 = 32
```

The order of A and B does not change the result.

### Matrix product

The at sign calls the matmul method. Cell (i, j) of the result is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B:

```text
1*5 + 2*7 = 19    1*6 + 2*8 = 22
3*5 + 4*7 = 43    3*6 + 4*8 = 50
```

The order matters. B times A gives other numbers. The inner sizes must agree, and the result has the rows of A and the columns of B.

### Which one a layer uses

A dense layer computes an activation of W times x plus b. Each output mixes all inputs with its own row of weights, which is the dot product inside a matrix product. The element-wise product appears in other places in training, for example when the learning rate scales a gradient, or when a mask zeroes some values. NumPy runs the matrix product with tuned BLAS routines written in C and Fortran, which the lesson measures as about 100 times faster than a Python loop over the same numbers.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 1:** Does the order of A and B matter in each case? Expected: no for the element-wise product, yes for the matrix product.
- **Level 2:** Which of the two operations does a learning rate step use? Expected: a scalar times the gradient, which is an element-wise scale.
- **Level 2:** Why is the at sign so much faster than a loop in Python? Expected: it calls BLAS routines in C and Fortran. The lesson gives about 100 times.
- **Level 3:** Someone writes the star for the layer and the code runs without an error. How is that possible? Expected: the shapes happened to be equal, so the element-wise product ran and gave wrong values with no error.

## Wrong answers

- "Both print the same matrix, the star is another spelling of the at sign." The two operations follow different rules and give different numbers.
- "The at sign is the element-wise product and the star is the matrix product." The at sign calls matmul, which forms dot products of rows and columns. The star works on matching positions.
- "A dense layer multiplies each weight by its input, so it is element-wise." Each output also sums over all inputs. That sum is the dot product inside a matrix product.

## Taught in

The [vectors and matrices lesson](../../../phases/01-math-foundations/02-vectors-matrices-operations/) works both products by hand and then with NumPy.

interviews.title: Score a tree node with Gini and with entropy
interviews.markdown:
A node in a classification tree holds 6 cats and 4 dogs. Give its Gini impurity and its entropy in bits, and explain how a tree uses either number to choose a split.

## Short answer

The class shares are 0.6 and 0.4. Gini is 1 minus the sum of squared shares, so 1 minus 0.36 minus 0.16, which is 0.48. Entropy is minus the sum of share times log base 2 of share, which comes to 0.971 bits. The tree tries every feature and threshold and keeps the split with the largest drop from the parent's impurity to the weighted impurity of the two children.

## Full answer

### The two numbers

```text
Gini    = 1 - (0.6^2 + 0.4^2) = 1 - (0.36 + 0.16) = 0.48
Entropy = -(0.6 * log2(0.6) + 0.4 * log2(0.4))
        = -(0.6 * -0.737 + 0.4 * -1.322)
        = 0.442 + 0.529 = 0.971 bits
```

Gini is the chance that a random sample at the node is labeled wrong when you label it by the node's class distribution. Entropy is the average surprise of the labels at the node. Both are 0 for a pure node. For a two class node with equal shares, Gini is 0.5 and entropy is 1.0 bit.

### How the tree uses them

The information gain of a split is the parent's impurity minus the weighted average of the children's impurity, where each child is weighted by its share of the samples. The algorithm is greedy: at each node it sorts each feature, tries every midpoint between distinct values as a threshold, and keeps the pair with the highest gain. Then it recurses into both children. Greedy splitting does not find the best tree, because that problem is NP-hard, but it works well in practice.

### Gini or entropy

On most data the two criteria pick the same splits and give trees of about the same depth. Gini has no logarithm, so it is a little cheaper to compute. Entropy connects the split to information theory: the split that minimizes the conditional entropy of the label given the feature is the split that removes the most uncertainty.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** What is the gain of a split that puts all the cats on one side and all the dogs on the other? Expected: the children are pure, so their impurity is 0 and the gain equals the parent's impurity, 0.48 for Gini.
- **Level 2:** Why weight the children by their sample share? Expected: a pure child with one sample should not count as much as a mixed child with the rest of the data.
- **Level 3:** How does the tree turn a continuous feature into candidate thresholds? Expected: sort the values and try the midpoint between each pair of distinct neighbors.
- **Level 3:** What stops the recursion before every leaf holds one sample? Expected: pre-pruning limits such as a maximum depth, a minimum number of samples per leaf, or a minimum gain, or post-pruning after the full tree is grown.

## Wrong answers

- "Gini is 0.6 times 0.4." That product is half of the two class Gini. The formula is 1 minus the sum of squared shares, which gives 0.48 here.
- "Entropy of a 6 to 4 node is 1 bit because there are two classes." One bit is the maximum, reached only at equal shares. Unequal shares give less, 0.971 bits here.
- "Pick the split with the lowest child impurity, and the parent does not matter." The parent's impurity is the same for every candidate split at that node, so the ranking is the same, but the gain is what the tree stores and reports as feature importance.

## Taught in

The [decision trees lesson](../../../phases/02-ml-fundamentals/04-decision-trees/) computes both criteria for this node, and the [information theory lesson](../../../phases/01-math-foundations/09-information-theory/) defines entropy and conditional entropy.

interviews.title: Why autograd adds gradients instead of setting them
interviews.markdown:
This is the multiply operation of a small autograd engine.

```python
def __mul__(self, other):
    other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
    out = Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other), '*')
    def _backward():
        self.grad += other.data * out.grad
        other.grad += self.data * out.grad
    out._backward = _backward
    return out
```

A contributor replaces both `+=` with `=`, with the comment that a gradient should be set, not added. The XOR training loop still runs and the loss still falls. What did the change break, and how do you prove it in one small test?

## Short answer

A value that feeds two or more operations receives a gradient from each consumer, and the chain rule says those contributions add. With assignment, the last consumer to run overwrites the others, so every shared node gets a wrong gradient, including each weight that the summed loss uses once per sample. A numerical gradient check exposes the error in one call.

## Full answer

### What the chain rule says about shared nodes

When y depends on x through two paths, the derivative of y with respect to x is the sum of the derivatives along each path. In the engine, a node that is used twice has two closures that write to its `grad`. The topological order runs every consumer before the node passes its gradient to its own children, so both closures run, and the second must add to the first.

### Why the loop still ran

In the XOR loop the loss is the sum of four squared errors, one per sample, and every weight takes part in all four forward passes. With assignment, each weight keeps only the contribution of the sample that ran last. That is still a direction that often points downhill, so the loss moves. The gradient is wrong for every parameter even so.

### The one-line test

```python
x = Value(3.0)
y = x * x
y.backward()
```

Here `self` and `other` are the same object. The correct gradient of x squared at 3 is 6.0. The two closures each add 3.0, which gives 6.0. With assignment the result is 3.0. The lesson's `gradient_check` does the same job for any expression: it compares the engine with a centered finite difference and reports the difference, which must be far below 1e-5.

### The other side of the same rule

Because gradients add, the training loop must set every `grad` back to 0.0 before each backward call. The lesson does this with a loop over the parameters. A framework does the same with a zero_grad call. Both habits come from the same fact: gradient storage is an accumulator.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why must the training loop set every gradient to zero before backward? Expected: gradients accumulate, so a second backward would stack onto the first; the loop sets each parameter's grad to 0.0.
- **Level 3:** Write the smallest expression that fails with assignment. Expected: a value multiplied by itself; the gradient at 3 must be 6.0, and assignment gives 3.0.
- **Level 3:** Why does the topological order matter for this bug? Expected: all consumers of a node must run before the node passes gradient on; with assignment the answer depends on which consumer ran last.
- **Level 4:** Where does the same accumulation rule show up in a framework you use? Expected: a tensor's grad accumulates across uses and across backward calls, which is why the optimizer's zero_grad runs before each step.

## Wrong answers

- "Assignment is fine because each node has one parent." A node that feeds two operations has two consumers in the graph, and a weight in a summed loss has one consumer per sample.
- "The loss still goes down, so the gradients are correct." A wrong gradient can still point partly downhill. Only a numerical check proves it.
- "Use a running average instead of a sum." The chain rule sums the path contributions. An average divides the true gradient by the number of consumers.

## Taught in

The [chain rule and autodiff lesson](../../../phases/01-math-foundations/05-chain-rule-and-autodiff/) builds the Value class and the gradient check that catches this bug.

interviews.title: A gradient check that fails for the wrong reason
interviews.markdown:
You add a new layer to a from-scratch network and run a gradient check. The relative error between the analytical and the numerical gradient is about 1e-3 for one weight. A teammate says the backward pass has a bug. Before you agree, how do you decide whether the fault is in the backward pass or in the check itself?

## Short answer

A relative error near 1e-3 is in the warning band, so first make the check trustworthy. Use the two-sided difference, set the step to the range from 1e-5 to 1e-7, run the check in float64, and compute the relative error with the max of both magnitudes in the denominator. If the error stays near 1e-3 or grows under those conditions, the backward pass is wrong; if it drops below 1e-5, the check was at fault.

## Full answer

### What the check computes

The numerical gradient for one weight is the centered difference: the loss at the weight plus h, minus the loss at the weight minus h, divided by 2h. Its truncation error shrinks with h squared, while the one-sided difference only shrinks with h. The relative error compares it with the analytical value:

```text
rel_error = |analytical - numerical| / max(|analytical|, |numerical|, 1e-8)
```

The lesson's thresholds: below 1e-7 is a clean match, below 1e-5 is acceptable, above 1e-3 points at a bug, and above 1 means the gradient is wrong.

### Ways the check lies

1. **Step too large.** The difference measures the slope of a chord, not the tangent. Shrink h.
