A failure at quantization invalidates only quantization and the server. The orchestrator reads the graph from the manifest, so the rollback set is computed, not remembered. A change to the tokenizer invalidates everything downstream; a change to the eval set invalidates only the ship decision.

### Why hashes make it safe

Artifacts live in an immutable store addressed by content hash, never by a name such as latest. A partial rerun checks whether each expected output already exists at the right hash and skips the stage if it does. That is also how a partial rollback saves most of the wall clock: stages one through eight stay cached while nine through twelve rerun. The pipeline lesson's exercise measures exactly that saving.

### What reproduce means

Reproducible: the same manifest, code and infrastructure give a checkpoint with equivalent downstream metrics. Deterministic: bit-identical output. Distributed reduce order, kernel nondeterminism and mixed precision rounding make modern training reproducible but not deterministic; weights differ at a level around 1e-5 between runs while the metrics do not move. The cure is to log the input hash, the output hash and the headline metrics per stage. If the code, recipe and source data hashes and the headline metrics match, the run is reproduced even when a weight artifact and the input hashes after it get new values, and a bit-level diff is the wrong debugging tool. The lesson's rule that the input hash, the output hash and the metrics all match holds in full for the stages with deterministic output, such as the tokenizer and the eval data; for a weight artifact, which cannot be bit-identical, the metrics carry the check.

### Budget as part of the plan

The pre-run cost estimate uses six times parameters times tokens for the training compute, divided by peak throughput and utilization, at the rental rate. If the estimate exceeds the cost gate the pipeline refuses to start. After each stage the remaining budget is rechecked, so an overrun in one stage changes the gate for the next instead of being discovered when the money is gone.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why not name artifacts by version string? Expected: two artifacts can share a name and differ in content; the hash is the identity, and a name like latest is a trap.
- **Level 4:** The reward model and the DPO policy both depend on the SFT checkpoint. What can run in parallel and what must wait? Expected: the two can run together after SFT; the refined policy waits for both, and its input hash must be a deterministic combination of both outputs.
- **Level 4:** A corrupted checkpoint is discovered after alignment finished. Which plan applies? Expected: the expensive class; take the last good pre-training checkpoint and rerun the medium and cheap stages, never the full pre-training.
- **Level 4:** A teammate reports that their replay has different weights. Is the run broken? Expected: not by itself; compare the code, recipe and source data hashes and the headline metrics, and only a mismatch there means the run is not reproduced.

## Wrong answers

- "Rerun from the start to be safe." The expensive stage costs weeks; the typed graph tells you exactly which stages are invalid.
- "Keep the latest checkpoint file and overwrite it each step." A mutable name cannot be verified or replayed; content addressing is what makes the rollback set trustworthy.
- "If the weights are not bit-identical, the pipeline is not reproducible." Distributed training is not deterministic; reproducibility is defined on the code, recipe and source data hashes and the metrics.

## Taught in

The [complete LLM pipeline lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/13-building-complete-llm-pipeline/) gives the three cost classes, the descendant rule, the content-addressed store and the distinction between reproducible and deterministic.

interviews.title: Put a model demo behind a public link safely
interviews.markdown:
A reviewer and a customer want to try your model from a link, on a phone, without your notebook. Each model call costs money. Design the demo: the input contract, the order of the checks, the controls for a public link, and what the log is allowed to keep.

## Short answer

Write the contract first: a string of 1 to 500 characters with no control characters, a model call with a known cost, and an output that includes a JSON error with a hint. Run the checks in order of cost, body size, access token, per-client token bucket, input validation, daily cap, and only then the model call. Return a stable error code with a message, a hint and a request id, and log the route, the status, the latency and the input length with a keyed hash of the client, never the text or the address.

## Full answer

### The contract

| Part | Question | Answer in the lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Input | What type, size and characters | A string of 1 to 500 characters, no control characters |
| Model call | How long and how much | Known latency and cost per call |
| Output | What the user sees on success and failure | A label and a reply, or a JSON error with a hint |

A notebook has no limit on any part. The demo sets one on each, and the server applies it to every client, because any client can skip the page.

### Checks in order of cost

1. Read the content length and refuse a body over 4,096 bytes before reading it.
2. Check the access token when one is required.
3. Take one token from the client's bucket; refuse with 429 and a `Retry-After` header when empty.
4. Parse and validate the body: JSON object, text present, inside the limit, no control characters, with 422 for a bad field.
5. Charge the daily cap; refuse with 503 and `Retry-After` when the day's budget is spent.
6. Call the model.

A bad request stops at the first failed check and costs almost nothing. The paid step is last, so only valid requests count against the cap.

### Controls once the link is public

| Risk | Control |
|---|---|
| One client floods | A token bucket per client: a capacity for bursts, a refill rate for the long run |
| Strangers find the link | An optional access token in the authorization header |
| Total cost grows | A daily usage cap over all clients, counted in windows of 86,400 seconds |
| Large or odd input | Body limit, text limit, control character check |
| Logs keep private input | Records with the input length and a keyed hash of the client |

A rate limit controls each client and not the total; a hundred polite clients can still spend the budget, which is what the cap is for.

### Errors a user can act on

Every error has the same shape: a stable `code` for clients and tests, a `message` with the numbers the user needs, a `hint` with one action, and a `request_id` that joins a user report to one log record. A stack trace does none of these jobs for a stranger.

### Feedback and streaming

The page disables the button while a request runs, shows the elapsed time, and shows the time to first token when it arrives, so the user can tell a slow model from a broken page and does not click again. Tokens stream as server-sent events over a POST body, not a GET URL, so the input never lands in an access log.

### What the log keeps

Route, status, error code, latency and input length, plus a keyed hash of the client address for per-client counts. Never the input text, never the raw path, never the address. The page tells users what is kept.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why does the daily cap run after validation and not before? Expected: so only valid requests count against the budget; a rejected request should not spend it.
- **Level 2:** Behind a reverse proxy every request has the proxy's address. What breaks? Expected: all users share one bucket; read the client address from a header that only your proxy sets and trust it from nowhere else.
- **Level 3:** Why send the input in a POST body instead of the URL for the event stream? Expected: servers and proxies write URLs into access logs, so a GET would store user text.
- **Level 3:** A framework builds the page for you. Which controls are still your job? Expected: the rate limit, the cost cap and log privacy; the frameworks save work on the form and the streaming, not on the risks of a public link.

## Wrong answers

- "Validate in the browser with a maximum length attribute." The browser helps honest users only; the server repeats every check.
- "A rate limit per client is enough to control cost." It bounds each client, not the sum; the daily cap bounds the total.
- "Log the full request so you can debug reports." The log then holds user text and addresses; a request id joins a report to a record without either.

## Taught in

The [model demo interfaces lesson](../../../phases/17-infrastructure-and-production/29-model-demo-interfaces/) gives the contract, the ordered checks, the token bucket, the usage cap and the private log.

interviews.title: Design cited search over ten repositories of code
interviews.markdown:
An engineering organization wants to ask questions across 10 repositories with about 2M lines of code and get answers that cite file and line. The index must stay fresh on every push. Design the ingestion, the retrieval, the answer step, the freshness path, and the evaluation, with the budgets you would commit to.

## Short answer

Parse each file into function and class nodes and chunk at those boundaries, give each chunk a dense embedding, sparse terms and a one-sentence summary, and store a graph of imports and calls between chunks. A query runs dense and sparse search in parallel, merges and deduplicates, reranks the top 50 with a cross-encoder to keep 10, and hands those to a long-context model that must cite every claim by file and line; uncited claims are dropped. A push triggers a symbol-level diff so only changed chunks re-embed, with a budget of under 60 seconds for a 50-file push. Quality is measured on 100 labeled cross-repo questions with MRR@10, nDCG@10, citation faithfulness and p50 and p99 latency.

## Full answer

### Ingestion

- A push webhook starts a worker that collects the changed files.
- A parser with grammars for the languages in the fleet extracts function and class nodes with their full source span. Chunks follow node boundaries, not fixed token windows.
- Each chunk gets three representations: a dense code embedding, sparse terms in a field-weighted index with symbol names weighted 4, bodies 1 and summaries 2, and a one-sentence summary written by a small model with the system preamble cached.
- A symbol graph records imports, calls and inheritance across files and repositories, used at query time to expand retrieval across repo boundaries.

The summary is the third retrievable modality: a user asks how something is authorized, the code says `check_permission`, and the summary says authorization.

### Retrieval and answer

1. Fire dense and sparse search in parallel, deduplicate by repository, path and symbol.
2. Rerank the top 50 with a cross-encoder and keep the top 10.
3. Call the synthesizer with the reranked chunks and a cached system prompt, requiring a file and line anchor on every claim.
4. Parse the output and check each anchor against the span at the indexed commit; a claim without an anchor, or with a span that is missing or does not support it, is re-asked or dropped. Only verified claims return.

Naive cosine search alone is poisoned by generated boilerplate, monorepo duplication and rarely imported symbols, which is why the hybrid search, the reranker and the graph exist.

### Freshness

On each webhook compute the symbol-level diff. Re-embed only the chunks whose text changed, recompute the import, call and inheritance edges of the changed symbols, and delete the chunks, summaries and edges of removed files and symbols from every store. The budget is a 50-file push searchable in under 60 seconds for the whole fleet, without reprocessing the 2M lines.

### Evaluation and budgets

| Weight | Criterion | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| 25 | Retrieval quality | MRR@10 and nDCG@10 on 100 held-out questions |
| 20 | Citation faithfulness | Share of claims with a verifiable file and line anchor |
| 20 | Latency and scale | p95 query latency at 10k QPS on the indexed corpus |
| 20 | Incremental indexing | Time from push to searchable on a 50-file commit |
| 15 | Answer formatting | Clickable citations, snippet previews, follow-up affordance |

A weekly rerun of the 100 questions with an alert on an MRR@10 drop above 5% catches drift in the index or the models.

### The service around it

The query path sits inside the production stack from the application lesson: a gateway with per-user limits, guardrails on input and output, streaming of the answer, structured logs per retrieval and synthesis step, and cost tracking that attributes the summary model, the embeddings, the reranker and the synthesizer separately.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why chunk at syntax nodes instead of fixed token windows? Expected: a window cuts functions in half and mixes neighbors; a node is one coherent unit with a stable symbol name to cite and deduplicate on.
- **Level 3:** What does the reranker add that the two retrievers cannot? Expected: it scores each query and candidate pair together, which is more accurate than cosine on separate embeddings, at a cost that only the top 50 can afford.
- **Level 4:** Generated boilerplate makes up a fifth of the corpus. What happens and what do you change? Expected: retrieval poisoning, where near-duplicate generated code crowds the results; flag generated chunks in the payload and down-weight them.
- **Level 4:** A question needs code from four repositories. Which component carries that? Expected: the symbol graph expands the candidate set across import and call edges, so the reranker sees chunks from repositories the first search missed.

## Wrong answers

- "A million-token context window replaces retrieval." Context helps but does not rank; cross-repo questions still need retrieval and citations.
- "Dense embeddings alone are enough for code." Exact symbol names need the sparse index, and the summary catches intent that the code text does not state.
- "Re-index the fleet on every push to keep it simple." Reprocessing 2M lines per commit blows the freshness budget; the diff keeps the index consistent at a fraction of the work.

## Taught in

The [RAG over a codebase capstone](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/02-rag-over-codebase/) gives the ingestion, the hybrid retrieval, the citation rule, the freshness budget and the rubric, and the [production LLM application lesson](../../../phases/11-llm-engineering/13-production-app/) gives the service around the query path.

interviews.title: Offline accuracy was fine and live accuracy is not
interviews.markdown:
A churn model scored well offline and does worse than the older, simpler model on live traffic. Serving features are computed by another team's service. You have a sample of logged serving requests. Design the triage: which comparisons you run, in which order, what each one isolates, and what the fix looks like for each cause you find.

## Short answer

Compare the same entity and time across three pairs. The online store read against the training join tests the whole system and should show zero skew when both read one definition. A fresh computation against the training join isolates staleness, and the second team's code path against a fresh computation isolates code differences such as window boundaries and defaults. Each pair gives a mismatch rate and a mean absolute difference per feature, and the fix for every cause is the same shape: one registry definition that both paths call, with logged serving features checked against it.

## Full answer

### The four causes

| Cause | What happens | Example from the lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Two code paths | Training and serving compute the feature differently | The serving window includes one extra day |
| Stale features | The served value has a different age than training saw | Training read weekly snapshots, serving computes fresh |
| Different defaults | The two paths fill a missing value differently | Training used 365 for no purchase yet, serving used -1 |
| Time travel | Training read a value from after the label time | A naive join took the newest snapshot |

### The three comparisons

1. Online store read against the training join. Both read the same materialized rows from one definition, so every feature should show a mismatch of zero. A nonzero result here means the store or the join itself is wrong.
2. Fresh computation against the training join. This isolates staleness. In the lesson's demo the fresh value differs on most requests: 83.0% mismatch for days since last purchase, 30.5% for the purchase count, 37.1% for spend. Fresher is not better here, because the model learned from values up to six days old.
3. Second code path against fresh computation. This isolates code. The demo shows 12.5% mismatch on both window counts, because the other team's window includes one extra day, and 5.5% mismatch on days since last purchase with a mean difference of 20.07, which comes only from new users where the defaults disagree, -1 against 365.

The check needs the same request keys on both sides, and it fails loudly when the keys differ or when there are no requests, because a missing request hides skew and an empty check proves nothing.

### The fixes

- Two code paths: delete the private copy; both services call the registry definition, and a change creates a new version that old models do not pick up.
- Stale features: match the serving age to the training age, or retrain on the fresher snapshots; a feature's freshness is part of its definition.
- Different defaults: one default in the registry, applied by one function in both paths.
- Time travel: the point-in-time join with the TTL, which the demo shows moves offline accuracy from an inflated 0.948 to an honest 0.893 and live accuracy from 0.763 to 0.876.

### Why the simpler model won live

The older model used features that both paths computed the same way. The new model trusted a feature whose live values came from a different window and a different default, so it saw inputs it never trained on.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Which comparison would you run first with one hour available? Expected: the first one; if the store read matches the training join, the system is consistent and the problem is elsewhere, and if not, every downstream check is moot.
- **Level 3:** The defaults differ only for new users. Why does the mismatch rate understate the damage? Expected: the rate is low because new users are few, but the difference per mismatch is huge, so the model's output for every new user is wrong.
- **Level 4:** The other team cannot change their service this quarter. What do you do? Expected: log their served features, train the next model on those logged values so training matches serving, and keep the skew check running so the gap is visible.
- **Level 4:** How does a created timestamp enter the triage? Expected: a backfill written today can read late-arriving data, so a strict join also drops rows created after the label time; otherwise the training path itself is skewed.

## Wrong answers

- "Fresh serving features are always better than training snapshots." The model learned the training freshness; a different age is skew in either direction.
- "A mismatch rate under a few percent is fine." A small rate with a large mean difference, as with the defaults, still breaks every affected prediction.
- "Compare offline accuracy with live accuracy and call it drift." Drift is a change over time; skew is a difference between two readers of the same feature at the same time, and the three comparisons tell them apart.

## Taught in

The [feature store lesson](../../../phases/02-ml-fundamentals/21-feature-stores-and-training-serving-skew/) names the four causes of skew and runs the three comparisons on logged requests.

interviews.title: Keep a chat service answering when the provider does not
interviews.markdown:
Design the request path of a chat service that calls a hosted model. Users leave when nothing appears for a few seconds, the provider returns rate limits and server errors at night, and the vector store behind retrieval sometimes times out. Cover what the user sees, how you retry, and what happens when each part fails.

## Short answer

Stream tokens over server-sent events so the first token appears in a few hundred milliseconds even though the full answer takes seconds. Retry provider failures with exponential backoff and jitter, capped at three retries, then fall through an ordered chain of models to a cached answer and finally a short unavailable message. Secondary systems degrade instead of failing the request: no retrieval context when the vector store is down, a direct model call when the cache is down, and a clear message when a guardrail blocks.

## Full answer

### Streaming

A response of a few hundred output tokens takes 3-8 seconds to finish. Without streaming the user watches a spinner for all of it. With streaming the first token arrives in 200-500ms, the total time is the same, and the perceived latency drops. Server-sent events are the default: one direction, over plain HTTP, consumed by the browser's event source or any HTTP client. Websockets are for two-way needs such as voice, and long polling is for clients that cannot do either.

### Three layers of failure

| Layer | Example | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Provider | 429 rate limit, 500 server error, timeout | Backoff with jitter, then the fallback chain |
| Model | Malformed JSON, invented function name | Retry once with the error in the prompt |
| Application | Vector store slow, cache down, guardrail exception | Degrade: skip the secondary system |

Backoff starts at one second, doubles on each attempt and adds random jitter so that many clients do not retry in step. Three retries is the cap; after that the request moves to the next model. Every external call has a timeout, with a default around 30s.

### The fallback chain

Primary model, then a cheaper or more available model, then a smaller one, then a cached response, then the unavailable message. Each step trades quality for availability. The user always gets something, and the log records which step answered so the cost tracker and the quality dashboard can attribute it.

### Degradation table

- 429: retry with backoff; queue the request and tell the user it is processing.
- 500: retry up to three times, then switch model; transparent to the user.
- Timeout: one retry with a shorter prompt or a smaller model.
- Malformed output: retry with the error attached, else return the raw text.
- Guardrail block: no retry; explain why the request was blocked.
- Vector store down: no retry on the store; answer without retrieval context.
- Cache down: no retry on the cache; call the model directly.

### The user-visible contract

The dashboard targets are a median under 2s and a p99 under 10s. Streaming moves the first-token time inside the median target even when the full response does not. A streamed response has one trap: the status line is sent before the first token, so a failure after that must be sent as an error event inside the stream.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why add jitter to the backoff? Expected: many clients that fail at once would otherwise retry at the same instants and reproduce the overload.
- **Level 2:** Why is a guardrail block not retried? Expected: the input is the problem; retrying the same input gives the same block and spends a call.
- **Level 3:** The fallback model has a different price. Where does that show up? Expected: in the cost tracker per request and per model, so the dashboard shows the cost of the outage, not only its rate.
- **Level 3:** The stream has started and the model fails. What can the server still do? Expected: send an error event inside the stream, because the HTTP status is already committed.

## Wrong answers

- "Retry until the provider answers." Unbounded retries pile up during an outage; cap them and fall through the chain.
- "If retrieval is down, fail the request so the answer stays grounded." A secondary system must not take down the primary flow; answer with reduced context and log it.
- "Buffer the whole response and send it at once for simplicity." The user sees nothing for seconds and leaves; the total time is the same either way.

## Taught in

The [production LLM application lesson](../../../phases/11-llm-engineering/13-production-app/) gives the streaming protocols, the three failure layers, the backoff schedule and the fallback chain.

interviews.title: When to say no to a model
interviews.markdown:
A product owner asks your team for "a model" to decide which support tickets get escalated. Before you design anything, what questions decide whether this should be a learned model at all, and what would make you answer with a rule instead?

## Short answer

I ask whether a short rule already reaches the goal, whether labels exist or can be collected, whether anyone will act on the prediction, whether the data at decision time holds the signal, and whether one error is acceptable. A model loses when a few conditions stay correct and explain themselves, when there are no labels, or when the cost of building and running the system exceeds the value of the better decisions. A model wins when the rule has grown long and fragile, because a learned model is easier to update than a complex heuristic.

## Full answer

### The cases against a model

| Condition | Why a rule wins |
|---|---|
| The logic fits in a few conditions and stays correct | Cheaper to run, test and explain |
| No labels and no practical way to collect them | Nothing to learn from |
| Nobody acts on the prediction | A better score changes nothing |
| The decision-time data does not contain the signal | The model cannot see what matters |
| One error is unacceptable and no person checks the output | A probabilistic system will be wrong sometimes |
| The system costs more than the better decisions are worth | Negative return |
| The problem changes faster than retraining | The model is always stale |

A lookup table or a threshold that covers 99% of cases is the right system, and adding a model raises maintenance cost for little gain.

### The cases for a model

The rules guide quoted in the design lesson says not to fear launching without machine learning, and also to prefer a model over a complex heuristic. The crossing point is when the rule has many branches, breaks on new cases, and nobody can say why it decides as it does. A learned model is retrained; a long rule is rewritten.

### How I would run the ticket case

1. Ask what the escalation decision is, who makes it, and when the features exist.
2. Build the rule the support team already uses, even if it lives in a spreadsheet, and measure it.
3. Set the minimum lift a model must show over that rule before any training.
4. Only then collect labels and train, and compare against the rule with the same metric.

The rule is also the safe default when the model service fails, so it is built first either way.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 1:** Where do labels for ticket escalation come from, and what is their delay? Expected: from past escalation decisions or outcomes, which arrive after the ticket closes; the delay sets how fresh the training data can be.
- **Level 2:** The team has no escalation history at all. What do you build first? Expected: the rule, with logging of the decision and its inputs, so labels start to accumulate.
- **Level 2:** A regulator requires that every escalation decision be explainable. What changes? Expected: either keep the rule or restrict the model to interpretable forms such as a small tree or a linear model.

## Wrong answers

- "A model always beats a rule given enough data." The rule can win when the features carry weak signal, and the lift must be measured, not assumed.
- "Collect data later; ship the model first." Without labels there is nothing to train on and nothing to evaluate against.
- "The heuristic baseline is just a sanity check." It is the real competitor and the safe default for failures.

## Taught in

The [introduction to machine learning](../../../phases/02-ml-fundamentals/01-what-is-machine-learning/) gives the decision flowchart for when not to use a model, and the [ML system design lesson](../../../phases/02-ml-fundamentals/19-ml-system-design/) lists the cases where a rule wins and sets the minimum lift.

interviews.title: Mean latency improved and the tail got worse
interviews.markdown:
Two changes shipped in one week: the target model moved to its next version, and a new customer whose traffic is mostly code was routed onto the same cluster. Speculative decoding has been on for months. Since then the mean inter-token latency fell 25 percent, the P99 rose 15 percent, and throughput at the usual concurrency is down. Diagnose it.

## Short answer

Both changes attack acceptance. The draft head was trained against the previous target version, so its distribution drifted and more drafts reject; the code traffic shifts the input distribution away from the general chat data the head was trained on, where acceptance falls into the 0.4 to 0.6 band. A rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll, two passes that serialize under a full batch, which is exactly a tail that worsens while the mean still improves. Read acceptance per traffic slice and per target version from the engine's speculative metrics, retrain or roll back to a head aligned with the new target, and gate speculation per request class.

## Full answer

### Why mean and tail move in opposite directions

Most requests still accept most drafts, so their inter-token latency falls and the mean improves. The requests that reject early pay the draft steps, the verify and a second target pass for the correction, and under a full batch those passes queue behind each other. The tail is where the rejected requests live. Watch P99, not P50.

### Cause one: a draft one version behind

A hidden-state draft is trained to predict a specific target's next token from that target's features. A new target version changes the features and the distribution, and the draft's agreement with it drops. The capstone's first exercise is to measure this degradation and to build the alert for it.

### Cause two: a domain the head never saw

A head trained on general chat sits at 0.6 to 0.8 acceptance there and at 0.4 to 0.6 on code, medical or legal traffic. Code tokens are predictable for a draft trained on code, and poorly predicted by one that was not. Below an acceptance of about 0.55 at high concurrency speculation is net negative, so the new customer may have pushed the cluster under the floor.

### The diagnosis

1. Pull accepted draft tokens and proposed draft tokens per request from the engine, divide the first by the second, and split by target version and by customer or request class. One number for the whole cluster hides both causes.
2. Compare the chat slice before and after the upgrade: if it fell, the version drift is real.
3. Compare the code slice against the chat slice at the same version: if it sits far lower, the domain shift is real.
4. Confirm the tail story by bucketing P99 by acceptance; the slow tail should be the low-acceptance slice.

### The fix

- Retrain the head against the new target version, or roll the target back until the aligned head is ready.
- Route the code customer to a plain decode pool, or train a code-specific head; the training job is light next to fine-tuning the target.
- Gate speculation per request class on measured acceptance, with an n-gram or draft-free fallback below the floor.
- Alert on acceptance per slice so the next version bump cannot ship without the draft.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why can the mean improve while throughput falls? Expected: the accepted requests get faster, but the rejected ones consume two target passes each, and at a full batch that extra work displaces other requests.
- **Level 4:** Design the alert in two sentences. Expected: compute acceptance per slice and per target version over a short window and compare against the baseline recorded at rollout; page when a slice crosses the floor or drops a fixed share from its baseline.
- **Level 4:** What is the fallback when acceptance drops on one slice only? Expected: switch that slice to an n-gram draft or to plain decoding while the head is retrained, and keep speculation where it still pays.
- **Level 4:** How does this change your release process? Expected: a target upgrade ships together with a draft trained against it, and the benchmark that gates the release reports acceptance and P99 per slice.

## Wrong answers

- "Increase the draft length to win back throughput." More drafts at low acceptance are mostly rejected and their cost is still paid; the tail gets worse.
- "Turn speculation off everywhere." The chat slice may still pay; gate by slice and fix the head.
- "The new target is just slower; speculation has nothing to do with it." A plain-decode benchmark of the new target settles that in minutes, and the mean improving while the tail worsens points at rejections.

## Taught in

The [speculative decoding server capstone](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/14-speculative-decoding-server/) sets the drift measurement and the fallback exercises, the [production EAGLE-3 lesson](../../../phases/17-infrastructure-and-production/05-eagle3-speculative-decoding/) explains the tail and the acceptance floor, and the [EAGLE-3 lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/15-speculative-decoding-eagle3/) explains why the draft is tied to one target version.

interviews.title: One step of byte-pair training and what it leaves behind
interviews.markdown:
Walk me through one training step of byte-pair encoding on a small corpus, and tell me what the trained artifact actually is.

## Short answer

Start with every word split into base symbols, bytes or characters. Count every adjacent pair across the corpus, weighted by how often each word appears, merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol with the next free id, rewrite every occurrence, and repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. The artifact is the ordered list of merges; the vocabulary follows from it, and the same list applied in the same order is what encoding uses later.

## Full answer

### A worked step

Corpus: "lower" 5 times, "lowest" 2 times, "newest" 6 times.

```text
l o w e r      (x5)
l o w e s t    (x2)
n e w e s t    (x6)

pair counts: (w,e): 13   (e,s): 8   (s,t): 8   (l,o): 7   (o,w): 7   (n,e): 6   (e,r): 5
merge (w,e) -> we

l o we r       (x5)
l o we s t     (x2)
n e we s t     (x6)
```

Recount, and the next step sees (we,s) and (s,t) tied at 8. The lesson's implementation breaks ties by sorting on the pair itself, so two runs over the same corpus produce the same table. After enough steps "west" exists as one symbol.

### The three facts the loop encodes

1. Frequency weighting makes the pairs of common words win early.
2. A pre-split on whitespace and punctuation keeps merges inside a word. A word-end marker also keeps "low" as a whole word distinct from "low" as the start of "lower".
3. The merge list is ordered. Encoding applies merges in training order, so the order is part of the artifact.

### Byte level

With bytes as the base, the first 256 ids are the byte values and merge k gets id 256 plus k. The cost of one step is linear in the corpus as a list of symbol sequences, and the sequences shrink as merges land, so a million words to ten thousand ids runs in seconds.

### What you ship

The merge table and the special-token table. The vocabulary of byte strings can be rebuilt from them.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 1:** Why weight pairs by word frequency instead of counting each distinct word once? Expected: the merges should serve the text the model will see, and common words appear many times.
- **Level 2:** Why must a tie in pair counts be broken deterministically? Expected: two training runs on the same corpus must produce the same table, or the same text would get different ids.
- **Level 2:** What happens to the encoded length of a sentence as the target vocabulary grows from 300 to 600? Expected: it falls, because more merges cover longer pieces; that curve is the compression curve.
- **Level 3:** Why split the corpus into words before you count pairs? Expected: without it, merges cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with whole phrases that do not generalize.

## Wrong answers

- "BPE picks the pair that makes the most meaningful piece." It picks the most frequent pair; meaning is a side effect, and the likelihood-based variant is a different algorithm.
- "The vocabulary is the artifact; the merge list can be discarded." Encoding needs the merges in order; the vocabulary alone does not say how to split new text.
- "All merges are chosen at once from the initial pair counts." Each merge changes the counts, so the loop recounts after every step.

## Taught in

The [tokenizers lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/01-tokenizers/) works the example, the [BPE capstone](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/30-bpe-tokenizer-from-scratch/) builds the loop with deterministic ties, and the [subword lesson](../../../phases/05-nlp-foundations-to-advanced/19-subword-tokenization/) names the three facts.

interviews.title: Three ways to build a subword vocabulary
interviews.markdown:
Three subword algorithms dominate: byte-pair encoding, WordPiece and Unigram. Contrast how each builds its vocabulary, tell me which one can give two different segmentations of the same word on purpose, and name the libraries you would reach for.

## Short answer

Byte-pair encoding merges the most frequent adjacent pair, bottom up. WordPiece also merges bottom up but scores a pair by the count of the merged piece over the product of the counts of its parts, so it prefers pairs that co-occur more than chance, and it marks continuation pieces with a double-hash prefix. Unigram works top down: it starts from a large candidate set, assigns each piece a probability, and prunes the pieces whose removal hurts the corpus likelihood least, which is why it can also sample alternative segmentations for regularization.

## Full answer

### The criteria side by side

```text
BPE merge criterion:        count(A, B)
WordPiece merge criterion:  count(AB) / (count(A) * count(B))
Unigram:                    prune the piece whose removal least lowers the corpus log-likelihood
```

The first asks which pair appears most. The second asks which pair appears together more often than you would expect from its parts. The third asks which pieces the corpus can best do without.

### Who uses what

| Algorithm | Direction | Marker | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Byte-pair encoding | merge up | leading space kept on word-initial pieces | most decoder families, with vocabularies of 50,257, 128,256 and more |
| WordPiece | merge up by likelihood ratio | `##` for continuation pieces | the classic encoder with 30,522 tokens |
| Unigram | prune down | `▁` for a space when trained without pre-tokenization | an encoder-decoder family with 32,000 tokens |

### Sampling segmentations

A Unigram model is probabilistic at inference. It can return the most likely segmentation or sample another one, which gives subword regularization during training: the same word arrives in several forms and the model learns pieces more robustly. The merge-based algorithms are deterministic.

### Libraries

One library trains vocabularies for either the merge or the prune algorithm directly on raw text, encoding the space as a visible symbol and needing no pre-tokenization, which is why it is the default for multilingual work. A second, Rust-backed encoder is fast and matches the vocabularies of a widely used API family, but it only encodes. A third library trains and serves both algorithms in one place.

### Picking

Training a monolingual model: byte-pair encoding. Training multilingual: Unigram with a character coverage near 0.9995. Serving against an existing API vocabulary: the encoder-only library. Edge inference with a small model: Unigram with a smaller vocabulary.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** What is subword regularization? Expected: training on sampled segmentations from a Unigram model so the same word appears in several forms.
- **Level 2:** What does the visible-space symbol buy? Expected: the space becomes an ordinary symbol, so the tokenizer needs no pre-tokenization and works for scripts without spaces.
- **Level 3:** Which algorithm and setting for a multilingual vocabulary? Expected: Unigram trained on raw text with character coverage near 0.9995, so rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown.
- **Level 3:** Why can an encode-only library not train your tokenizer? Expected: it ships pre-built vocabularies and a fast encoder; the training step lives in the other two libraries.

## Wrong answers

- "WordPiece and byte-pair encoding give the same vocabulary on the same corpus." The criteria differ, so the merges differ; the likelihood ratio favors surprising pairs over merely frequent ones.
- "Unigram is deterministic like the merge algorithms." It is probabilistic and can sample segmentations on purpose.
- "The library that encodes the space as a symbol is itself an algorithm." It is a library that trains either the merge or the prune algorithm on raw text.

## Taught in

The [subword tokenization lesson](../../../phases/05-nlp-foundations-to-advanced/19-subword-tokenization/) contrasts the three algorithms and the libraries, and the [tokenizers lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/01-tokenizers/) gives the merge criteria and the vocabulary sizes.

interviews.title: The notebook works and the service never stops talking
interviews.markdown:
A fine-tuned chat model answers well in the training notebook. The deployed service, with identical weights, returns rambling text that runs until the token limit. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find?

## Short answer

At the flat token sequence the model actually receives, not at the list of messages. A chat model was trained on one exact layout of role markers, special tokens and newlines; a missing newline, a swapped marker or an extra space puts the input outside the training distribution, and the end-of-turn token stops being predicted. Print the token ids of the same request from both paths and diff them, and check that the special tokens arrived as their reserved ids and not as the bytes that spell them.

## Full answer

### The model never sees the JSON

The service holds a list of role and content pairs. The model sees one flat sequence built by the chat template, which inserts markers such as a begin-of-text token, a header for each role and an end-of-turn token after each message, with specific newlines between them. Every model family lays this out differently. The template is part of the model, in the same way the vocabulary is.

### The three ways it breaks

1. **A different template.** The service used a generic layout or an older version. Each message now sits in a frame the model never saw, and the end-of-turn marker it learned is absent or misplaced, so it never predicts the stop token.
2. **Special tokens spelled out.** Special tokens must be matched exactly before the merge loop and mapped to fixed ids. If the service built the prompt as plain text and encoded it with the allow flag off, the marker string became ordinary bytes and pieces. The model sees text that looks like a marker and is not one.
3. **Stop token mismatch.** The service stops on the generic end-of-sequence id while the model emits its end-of-turn id. Generation continues past the real end.

### The check that settles it

```text
ids_notebook = tokenizer(chat_template(messages))
ids_service  = ids the service sent to the engine
diff the two lists; the first difference is the bug
```

Then decode each id back to its string and look for a marker that decoded as several pieces instead of one reserved id. If the two lists match, the input is fine and the stop token is next: compare the stop ids in the service config with the end-of-turn id that the template puts after each message.

### The fix

Use the model's own template function, pass special tokens through the reserved-id path, and configure the stop token to the id the template ends a turn with. Freeze the tokenizer file and the template together with the weights.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** What does the end-of-turn token do at inference? Expected: it is the model's signal that the answer is complete; the server must stop on that id, or generation runs to the limit.
- **Level 3:** A user types the literal string of a special token into the chat box. What should happen? Expected: with the allow flag off it becomes ordinary bytes, which is the safe default for user text; with it on, the user could inject a control marker.
- **Level 3:** How do you test a template implementation? Expected: build the sequence for a fixed message list and compare it id by id with the output of the model's own template code.
- **Level 4:** The template is correct and the ids still differ between notebook and service. What else? Expected: a different tokenizer file version, a different normalization step, or a different setting for adding special tokens at the start; hash the tokenizer file and compare the flags.

## Wrong answers

- "The sampling temperature is too high in the service." Temperature changes which token is picked, not whether the stop token is ever predicted; the ids differ before sampling.
- "The fine-tune overfit." The same weights behave in the notebook; the difference is in the input layout.
- "Trim the output on the client." That hides the symptom and the model still wastes compute on text it should not generate.

## Taught in

The [tokenizer build lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/02-building-a-tokenizer/) shows the templates and the special-token path, the [BPE capstone](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/30-bpe-tokenizer-from-scratch/) explains the allow flag, and the [subword lesson](../../../phases/05-nlp-foundations-to-advanced/19-subword-tokenization/) lists the drift and whitespace pitfalls.

interviews.title: Bake in the draft, train it after, or borrow a small model
interviews.markdown:
You are about to pretrain a model that will later serve a large volume using speculative decoding. Three ways to get a draft are on the table: bake sequential multi-token modules into pretraining, train a hidden-state draft head after pretraining, or reuse a small model of the same family. Give the decision with its costs, and name the gate you measure before you ship the flag.

## Short answer

If I control pretraining and the hidden size is at least 4096, I bake in the sequential modules: about 10 percent slower training buys a denser supervision signal and a draft that accepts 80 percent or more at depth one. If the weights already exist, I train a post-hoc head on the verifier's features with about 60 to 200B tokens; it is backward compatible and reaches 0.88 to 0.92 acceptance on general chat. A same-family small model needs no training and sits around 0.55 to 0.70. Whatever I pick, the gate is measured acceptance on my own traffic mix at production concurrency, with the flag off below about 0.55 and the tail latency watched, not the mean.

## Full answer

### The three options

| Option | When trained | Works with existing weights | Draft parameters | Acceptance | Extra benefit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sequential modules in pretraining | during pretraining | no | one block plus a projection per depth | 0.80 and above at depth one | denser training signal |
| Post-hoc head on verifier features | after pretraining | yes | one or two layers, trained on about 60 to 200B tokens | 0.88 to 0.92 on chat | none beyond speed |
| Same-family small model | none | yes | a whole small model | 0.55 to 0.70 | none, and it costs memory |

### The decision tree

1. **Do you own pretraining?** If yes and the model is large enough, the modules are the only option that improves the model and the serving at once; the report that introduced them measured about 1.8 times generation throughput from the draft alone. At a 1B scale the overhead hurts more than it helps.
2. **Do the weights already exist?** Then the post-hoc head. It is a light training job compared with the verifier, and it does not touch the verifier's outputs.
3. **No training budget at all?** The small model, as a prototype, knowing the acceptance ceiling is low and the second model takes memory.

### The gate

Speculation is opt-in on the production engine, and the production lesson's rule is that flipping the flag without measuring acceptance on real traffic is an anti-pattern. The plan:

1. Serve the target plain and record time to first token, inter-token latency and throughput at the target concurrency.
2. Enable the draft and rerun the same benchmark.
3. Read accepted draft tokens and proposed draft tokens per request from the engine and divide the first by the second to get acceptance.
4. Below about 0.55 at production concurrency, disable the flag or train a domain-specific head.
5. Confirm that the tail inter-token latency did not get worse, because a rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll.

### Traffic mix

A head trained on general chat sits at 0.6 to 0.8 there and falls to 0.4 to 0.6 on code, medical or legal traffic. Weight the acceptance by traffic share before you decide, and measure each slice on its own; a blended number can hide a slice where speculation is net negative. The capstone's exercise asks exactly this for a 70 percent chat and 30 percent code mix with acceptances of 0.7 and 0.4.

### Operate it

Acceptance drifts when the target changes version and the draft does not, so alert on it per slice, and keep a draft-free or n-gram fallback for the slices where the head stops paying.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** The traffic is 70 percent chat at 0.7 acceptance and 30 percent code at 0.4. How do you decide? Expected: weight by traffic share, then check each slice against the floor; code alone is below it, so route code to a plain decode or train a code head.
- **Level 4:** The target gets a new version next quarter. What happens to each option? Expected: the baked-in modules move with the model; the post-hoc head must be retrained against the new target; the small model drifts further; alert on acceptance per version.
- **Level 4:** What does a hidden-state head read in the current generation? Expected: features from several target layers, not only the last, which is part of why acceptance rose.
- **Level 4:** Where does the small-model option still win? Expected: a prototype with no training budget, or a CPU deployment where the engine ships only the plain draft path.

## Wrong answers

- "Always use the latest hidden-state draft; it is strictly best." It needs training against your target and its acceptance on domain traffic can fall to 0.4; the baked-in modules give you a draft and a better model if you own pretraining.
- "Bake the modules in later with a fine-tune." They are a pretraining choice; an existing dense model gets a post-hoc head instead.
- "Pick by the speedup on a public benchmark." Acceptance depends on your traffic; the gate is measured on your own mix at your concurrency.

## Taught in

The [multi-token prediction lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/18-multi-token-prediction/) and the [EAGLE-3 lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/15-speculative-decoding-eagle3/) give the two trained options and their costs, the [production EAGLE-3 lesson](../../../phases/17-infrastructure-and-production/05-eagle3-speculative-decoding/) sets the measurement gate, and the [speculative decoding server capstone](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/14-speculative-decoding-server/) covers drift and fallback.

interviews.title: How a grammar edits the logits and why it can be faster
interviews.markdown:
A classifier prompt asks for one of three labels and the model answers with a paragraph, so the parser crashes. Three layers of fix exist. Explain how the strongest one works at the level of the logits, and why it is often faster than free generation, not slower.

## Short answer

Prompting asks nicely, a vendor's structured-output API does it on the server, and constrained decoding does it locally by editing the logits. At each step a logit processor computes which vocabulary tokens can advance the target grammar, a JSON schema, a regex or a context-free grammar compiled to a state machine, and sets every other logit to minus infinity, so the softmax puts probability only on valid continuations and an invalid output is unreachable. It can be faster because the search space shrinks and because tokens that the grammar forces, such as a fixed key name, are emitted without a model step.

## Full answer

### The three layers

1. **Prompting.** "Return only the JSON object." The lesson puts this at about 80 percent compliance on strong models and lower on small ones. Not a contract.
2. **Native structured output.** The provider runs the constraint on its side. Reliable for supported schemas; locked to that provider.
3. **Constrained decoding.** The constraint runs in your own decoding loop and works with any local model.

### The loop

```python
def generate_constrained(model, tokenizer, prompt, fsm):
    ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt)
    state = fsm.initial_state
    while not fsm.is_accept(state):
        logits = model.next_token_logits(ids)
        valid = fsm.valid_tokens(state, tokenizer)
        logits = mask_logits(logits, valid)
        tok = sample(logits)
        ids.append(tok)
        state = fsm.transition(state, tok)
    return tokenizer.decode(ids)
```

The state machine tracks how much of the grammar is satisfied. `valid_tokens` returns the vocabulary tokens that keep the machine on an accepting path; the mask sets the rest to minus infinity. The vocabulary is about 100k tokens, so the mask is computed per state ahead of time.

### State machine or grammar engine

A regex or a flat JSON schema compiles to a finite-state machine with a constant-time lookup of valid tokens per state. Recursive schemas, nested comments or a syntax tree, need a context-free grammar engine, which handles recursion at near-zero decoding overhead in current implementations. Inference servers expose both as guided decoding.

### Why it can be faster

Fewer candidate tokens means a smaller effective search at each step. More important, long stretches of the output are fully determined by the grammar: the opening brace, a quoted key, the colon. A good implementation skips the model for those tokens and only calls it where the grammar leaves a choice.

### The library that does not touch logits

A retry-based client formats the schema into the prompt, parses the output, and retries on a validation failure, 3 times by default. It works across providers, and each retry costs latency and money. It is a different mechanism, not a weaker version of the same one.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** When does a finite-state machine not suffice? Expected: for recursive schemas; the machine flattens recursion to a fixed depth, and a context-free grammar engine is needed.
- **Level 3:** What does a provider's plain JSON mode guarantee, and what does it not? Expected: valid JSON syntax, not conformance to your schema; always send a full schema.
- **Level 3:** How does the retry library differ from the logit processor? Expected: it never changes the model's distribution; it validates after the fact and retries, which adds latency and cost per failure.
- **Level 4:** The schema has an enum with 10,000 options and compilation times out. What do you do? Expected: predict a short list of candidates with a retriever first, then constrain the decode to those.

## Wrong answers

- "Constrained decoding makes the answer correct." It makes the answer valid for the grammar; a well-formed wrong answer still passes.
- "Checking the grammar at every token makes generation slower." The valid-token sets are precomputed per state, and forced tokens skip the model, so it is often faster.
- "Enough examples in the prompt reach full compliance." The lesson's figure for prompting alone is about 80 percent; a contract needs the logits or the server.

## Taught in

The [structured outputs lesson](../../../phases/05-nlp-foundations-to-advanced/20-structured-outputs-constrained-decoding/) builds the logit processor and compares the three layers.

interviews.title: Design the tokenizer for a multilingual coding model
interviews.markdown:
You are starting a 7B model that must serve many languages and also be strong at code. Design its tokenizer: the algorithm, the library, the vocabulary size, the coverage settings, and the validation plan you would gate the training run on.

## Short answer

Train a byte-fallback subword vocabulary on a corpus that mirrors the target mix of languages and code, with a pre-tokenizer that keeps leading spaces and separates digits and punctuation so that code tokenizes cleanly. For a model in the 1 to 10B range the heuristic is 50 to 100k tokens, and the multilingual requirement pushes to the top of that range or beyond it; set the character coverage near 0.9995 so that rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown. Gate on tokens per word per language, the unknown rate, the compression ratio against a reference encoder and a byte-exact round trip, and freeze the tokenizer file hash in CI before the first training step.

## Full answer

### Algorithm and library

The lesson's table points to the prune-based algorithm trained on raw text for multilingual work, because it needs no language-specific pre-tokenization and handles scripts without spaces, and to the merge-based algorithm for monolingual corpora. For a mixed requirement either works if the corpus is right; the corpus mix decides more than the algorithm. Use a library that trains, not one that only encodes against someone else's vocabulary. Keep byte fallback on in either case so that no input is ever unknown.

### Vocabulary size

| Model scale | Heuristic |
|---|---|
| under 1B | about 32k |
| 1 to 10B | 50 to 100k |
| multilingual or frontier | 200k and above |

A 7B model with many scripts sits at the top of the middle row. Each added row is an embedding to learn, and the embedding matrix at 128,000 rows by 4,096 dimensions is about 524M parameters, so the size is a budget decision and not a constant. The payoff is fertility: an English-heavy vocabulary gives other scripts 2 to 3 tokens per word or worse, and non-Latin text can cost 5 to 10 times more tokens; the larger multilingual vocabulary is what repairs that.

### Coverage and code

- Character coverage near 0.9995 for a mixed corpus; refuse anything under 0.995 when rare scripts are present.
- Byte fallback for everything the coverage still misses.
- A pre-tokenizer that keeps the leading space on words, splits digit runs and punctuation, and handles whitespace runs, so that indentation and operators in code become stable pieces. Chinese characters are 3 bytes each and need merges of their own, so the corpus must contain enough of them.
- Reserve the special tokens and the chat markers at the start, with fixed ids that no merge can produce.

### The corpus

Sample the training text for the tokenizer in the proportions you want the model to be good at. A domain vocabulary can also be trained on the code corpus and merged with the base vocabulary. A tokenizer trained on an English-heavy sample will under-serve every other script for the life of the model.

### The validation plan

1. Tokens per word, per language and for code, on held-out text; this is the fertility table you publish.
2. Unknown rate, which must be zero with byte fallback.
3. Compression ratio against a reference encoder on the same held-out text.
4. Round trip, encode then decode, on all of it, including emoji and literal special-token strings. Byte-exact when the tokenizer has no normalizer; with a normalizer such as NFKC, compare against the normalized text.
5. A frozen tokenizer file hash and golden token ids in CI, so that nothing drifts between training and serving.

Flag a monolingual vocabulary under 16k as under-specified, and refuse to ship a vocabulary without the hash check.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why does the corpus mix matter more than the algorithm choice? Expected: the merges or the pruned pieces follow the frequencies in the training text, so a script that is rare in the sample gets few pieces whatever the algorithm.
- **Level 4:** What does whitespace handling do to code? Expected: indentation is runs of spaces or tabs; a pre-tokenizer that keeps whitespace runs as their own chunks lets them become stable tokens instead of being glued to the next word.
- **Level 4:** The team wants to change the vocabulary after six months of training. What do you tell them? Expected: the embeddings and every weight were trained against the current ids; a change means a retrain, which is why the tokenizer decision is gated before the first step.
- **Level 4:** How do you report the tokenizer with the model? Expected: the fertility table per language, the size and coverage of the vocabulary, the special-token list and the file hash.

## Wrong answers

- "Pick 32k because earlier models used it." That size served monolingual models under 1B; a 7B multilingual coding model pays the tax in every language.
- "Set character coverage to 1.0 to be safe." Full coverage spends vocabulary on characters seen once; near 0.9995 with byte fallback keeps rare scripts without wasting rows.
- "Train on English now and add the other languages later." The vocabulary cannot change after training without a retrain; the languages must be in the tokenizer corpus from the start.

## Taught in

The [subword tokenization lesson](../../../phases/05-nlp-foundations-to-advanced/19-subword-tokenization/) gives the picking table, the size heuristic, the coverage rule and the validation plan, the [tokenizers lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/01-tokenizers/) does the embedding and fertility arithmetic, and the [tokenizer build lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/02-building-a-tokenizer/) covers pre-tokenization, byte counts and special tokens.

interviews.title: Why a draft that reads hidden states accepts more
interviews.markdown:
Walk the line from a separate small draft model to the current generation of hidden-state drafts. What limitation did each step remove, and why does feeding the draft the verifier's internal features help so much?

## Short answer

A separate small model from the same family accepts around 0.6 of its tokens, because its distribution drifts from the verifier's. The first hidden-state draft replaces it with a one or two layer network that reads the verifier's last-layer features, so the draft starts from the verifier's own representation and acceptance rises to 0.7 to 0.8. The second generation proposes a tree of candidates and verifies every branch in one pass with a tree-shaped attention mask, lifting acceptance per accepted-path token above 0.85. The third drops the feature-matching loss, trains on direct token prediction, and feeds the draft its own previous outputs during training, which removes exposure bias and reaches 0.88 to 0.92.

## Full answer

### The progression

| Generation | Draft | Acceptance | Training cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Separate small model | an independently trained smaller model | 0.55 to 0.70 | none |
| Extra heads on the verifier | several output heads predicting positions ahead | 0.65 to 0.75 | about 1B supervised tokens |
| First hidden-state draft | one transformer layer on the verifier's last hidden state | 0.70 to 0.80 | about 60B tokens |
| Dynamic draft tree | the same plus a tree of candidates | 0.80 to 0.88 | about 60B tokens |
| Multi-layer features plus training-time test | fuses several verifier layers; trained on its own outputs | 0.88 to 0.92 | about 60 to 200B tokens |

### Why the hidden state helps

A separate draft re-derives from raw tokens what the verifier has already computed. The verifier's last hidden state at position t is a rich summary of the prefix, and a tiny network that reads it predicts the verifier's next token far better than a small model that reads only the token ids. The draft becomes a reader of the verifier instead of an imitation of it.

### What the tree adds

A linear chain of drafts dies at the first miss. A tree proposes several candidates at each depth, grows wider where the draft is uncertain and stays narrow where it is confident, and the verifier scores every node in one forward pass with a mask that lets each node attend only to its ancestors. The longest accepted path wins. Verification cost barely moves, because it is still one forward pass.

### What the third generation fixes

The earlier hidden-state drafts were trained to match the verifier's features, which capped how much extra data could help. The third generation trains on token prediction directly, and during training it feeds the draft its own previous predictions over several steps, the way it runs at inference. That aligns the training inputs with the inference inputs and stops error accumulation, the same fix that scheduled sampling gave sequence models. The paper reports up to 6.5 times end-to-end on chat and a 38 percent throughput gain at a batch of 64 on a production engine.

### The draft is only as good as its traffic

A general-purpose draft head trained on chat data drops to 0.4 to 0.6 acceptance on code, medical or legal traffic. A domain-specific head recovers it, and training one is a light job next to fine-tuning the verifier.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why did matching the verifier's features cap the first generations? Expected: the feature loss asks the draft to reproduce hidden states rather than predict tokens, so more training data stopped helping; the third generation trains on tokens.
- **Level 3:** What is exposure bias in this setting? Expected: the draft was trained on teacher-forced verifier inputs and run on its own outputs; the mismatch compounds over the draft steps.
- **Level 4:** What does the tree cost? Expected: a non-causal attention mask that follows the tree topology, extra stored keys and values for the tree nodes, and scheduler complexity; the verifier still runs once.
- **Level 4:** How do you compare the extra-heads design with the hidden-state draft? Expected: no second model to deploy and simpler serving, against a somewhat lower acceptance and a supervised fine-tuning stage on the verifier.

## Wrong answers

- "A larger separate draft model is the main lever." Alignment with the verifier matters more than size; a one-layer draft on hidden states beats a far larger independent model.
- "The hidden-state draft changes the verifier's output distribution to gain acceptance." The rejection rule keeps the output exact; the draft only changes how often it is right.
- "A tree needs one verifier pass per branch." All branches are verified in one pass under the tree mask.

## Taught in

The [EAGLE-3 lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/15-speculative-decoding-eagle3/) walks the progression and the training-time test, the [Phase 10 speculative decoding lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/25-speculative-decoding/) explains feature reuse and tree verification, the [Phase 7 lesson](../../../phases/07-transformers-deep-dive/16-speculative-decoding/) introduces the draft families, and the [production EAGLE-3 lesson](../../../phases/17-infrastructure-and-production/05-eagle3-speculative-decoding/) covers domain drift.

interviews.title: Why the encoder replays the merge list in order
interviews.markdown:
At encode time a BPE tokenizer holds the complete merge table. Why does it have to replay the merges in the order they were learned, and what goes wrong when two merges could fire at the same spot?

## Short answer

Encoding must reproduce what training did to the same text, and training saw the merges one at a time in that order. If merge one created "th" and merge five created "the" from "th" plus "e", then "the" can only form after "th" exists. When two merges could apply at one position, the one with the lower rank, learned earlier, wins; change that rule and the same text yields different ids, so the model sees a distribution of ids it was never trained on.

## Full answer

### The naive encoder

```python
def encode_bpe(word, merges):
    symbols = list(word) + ["</w>"]
    for a, b in merges:
        i = 0
        while i < len(symbols) - 1:
            if symbols[i] == a and symbols[i + 1] == b:
                symbols = symbols[:i] + [a + b] + symbols[i + 2:]
            else:
                i += 1
    return symbols
```

It walks the whole table for every word, so the cost is the word length times the number of merges. Correct for a merge table trained on characters, and slow.

### The rank-based encoder

The capstone version starts from the byte split and repeats: find the applicable merge with the lowest rank anywhere in the current sequence, apply it, and scan again, until no merge in the table applies. Production encoders keep the same semantics with a rank lookup and a priority queue of candidate pairs, which runs in close to linear time.

### Why the rule is the contract

The training loop and the encoder share the merge table, and that sharing is the whole contract. Training merged the most frequent pair first, so an input that contains both halves of an early merge was always merged that way in the training data. An encoder that prefers a later merge, or the longest piece, produces a segmentation the model never saw. Nothing crashes; the ids are simply different.

### What special tokens do here

Reserved strings such as the end-of-text marker are matched exactly before the merge loop runs and mapped to fixed ids. They never take part in a merge, so no table order can split or join them.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 2:** Why is the naive loop slow? Expected: it scans the full merge table for every word, so the cost grows with the table size times the word length.
- **Level 3:** How do production encoders get close to linear time? Expected: a rank lookup for each adjacent pair and a priority queue that always surfaces the lowest-ranked applicable merge.
- **Level 3:** Two tokenizers were trained on different corpora to the same vocabulary size. Do they give the same ids? Expected: no; different corpora give different merge tables and different ranks.
- **Level 3:** What test pins the order? Expected: encode a held-out word and compare with recorded ids; the capstone's tests also pin the round trip and the special-token reservation.

## Wrong answers

- "Greedily take the longest token in the vocabulary that matches." That is a different algorithm and gives a different segmentation from the training run.
- "Order does not matter because merges commute." A later merge depends on the symbols that earlier merges created, so they do not commute.
- "Sort the merges by token length." Length is not rank; a long piece may have been learned early and a short one late.

## Taught in

The [tokenizers lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/01-tokenizers/) explains the ordered table, the [BPE capstone](../../../phases/19-capstone-projects/30-bpe-tokenizer-from-scratch/) implements the rank-based encoder, and the [subword lesson](../../../phases/05-nlp-foundations-to-advanced/19-subword-tokenization/) gives the naive loop and its cost.

interviews.title: Which multi-token design gives a free draft
interviews.markdown:
A pretraining team wants to supervise each position on more than the next token. One design puts several independent output heads on the backbone. Another chains small modules, one per extra depth. Which design gives you a usable speculative draft at inference, and what does it cost during training?

## Short answer

The chained design. Module k takes the previous depth's hidden state and the embedding of the actual next token, runs its own small transformer block, and reuses the shared embedding and the shared output head, so its prediction of the token at t plus k plus 1 is conditioned on the token at t plus k, which is the same causal chain a decoder follows and lets the module draft tokens at inference with acceptance at depth one of 80 percent or more for about 1.8 times throughput. Independent heads all read the same hidden state and cannot condition on each other. The training cost is about 10 percent slower pretraining and about 14 h squared parameters per module, with a loss weight of 0.3 early and 0.1 later.

## Full answer

### The sequential recipe

For a prefix through position i, depth zero is the main backbone, and depth k builds on depth k minus 1:

```text
h_i^(k) = T_k( M_k · concat( RMSNorm(h_i^(k-1)), RMSNorm(E(t_{i+k})) ) )
logits_{i+k+1} = Out( h_i^(k) )
L_k = cross-entropy( logits_{i+k+1}, t_{i+k+1} )
L_MTP = (lambda / D) · sum over k of L_k
```

`E` is the embedding table and `Out` is the output head, both shared with the main model. `M_k` folds the previous hidden state and the next token's embedding into one vector. `T_k` is one transformer block. The total loss is the main next-token loss plus `L_MTP`, with lambda at 0.3 for the first 10 percent of training and 0.1 afterward.

### Why the chain matters

To predict two tokens ahead, module one sees what the next token actually was. At inference you feed it the drafted token instead, and it predicts the one after. That is exactly how a hidden-state draft works, so the trained module is a draft network for free. Parallel heads fire from one hidden state, so head two cannot use head one's answer. A verifier can still check their guesses, but they are accepted less often.

### The accounting

Per module: the projection is `2 h^2`, the block is about `12 h^2` for attention and a gated MLP, so about `14 h^2`. At a hidden size of 7168 and one module that is about 720M on paper; the published figure is 14B on a 671B main model, about 2 percent, because the module's MLP inherits the expert structure of the main model. The embedding and head add nothing, because they are shared.

### What you get

1. A denser training signal: every hidden state is supervised on D plus 1 targets, and the report shows consistent gains on reasoning, math and code evaluations.
2. A draft at inference with 80 percent or more acceptance at depth one, for about 1.8 times generation throughput, and the training-time cost is paid back the first time the model serves.

### Against a post-hoc draft

| | Post-hoc hidden-state draft | Baked-in modules |
|---|---|---|
| When trained | after pretraining | during pretraining |
| Works with existing weights | yes | no, retrain |
| Draft parameters | one or two layers | one block plus a projection |
| Acceptance | 0.88 to 0.92 | 0.80 and above at depth one |
| Benefit beyond speed | none | denser training signal |

Use the baked-in design when you control pretraining and the hidden size is at least 4096; at a 1B scale the overhead hurts more than it helps. Use the post-hoc draft when the weights already exist.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 3:** Why share the embedding and the output head with the main model? Expected: no extra parameters, and the module predicts in the same vocabulary space as the backbone.
- **Level 3:** Why is the published parameter overhead larger than the `14 h^2` estimate? Expected: the module's MLP has the same expert structure as the main model, which multiplies its parameters.
- **Level 4:** With two modules, what does the second one take as input? Expected: the first module's hidden state and the embedding of the token two ahead, to predict the token three ahead.
- **Level 4:** A team wants to add this to an existing dense model by fine-tuning a new head. Your answer? Expected: the module is not trained and the backbone was not shaped by the extra loss; the lesson's position is that it needs a pretraining run, and a post-hoc draft is the right tool for existing weights.

## Wrong answers

- "The extra loss replaces next-token prediction." It is added to the main loss with a small weight; the main objective stays.
- "The module can be bolted onto a trained model with a quick fine-tune." The design is a pretraining choice; existing weights get a post-hoc draft instead.

## Taught in

The [multi-token prediction lesson](../../../phases/10-llms-from-scratch/18-multi-token-prediction/) gives the sequential recipe, the loss, the parameter accounting and the comparison with post-hoc drafts.

interviews.title: The same prompt costs more tokens in Korean
interviews.markdown:
A customer in Korea reports that the same prompt uses up far more of the context window than the English version, and the bill is higher too. Why does this happen, and what does a model builder do about it?

## Short answer

The vocabulary was trained on English-heavy text, so its merges cover English and other scripts fall back to short pieces or raw bytes. Korean averages 2 to 3 tokens per word on an older vocabulary, and non-Latin text can cost 5 to 10 times more tokens than English for the same meaning; a Chinese character is 3 bytes in UTF-8, so without merges each character is several tokens. The builder's fix is a larger vocabulary trained on multilingual data, which is why one model family grew its vocabulary from 32K to 128K.

## Full answer

### Where the tokens go

A byte-level tokenizer never fails, but it only compresses what it has merges for. Each Chinese character is 3 bytes, Japanese characters are 3 to 4 bytes, an emoji is 4 bytes and can take 5 tokens. If the training corpus held little of a script, the merge table has few pieces for it, and the text stays close to one token per byte.

### What the customer feels

- The context window is a token budget, so the same document fits less often.
- Pricing is per token, so the same request costs more.
- Latency is per generated token, so answers in that script are slower.

The lesson's phrase is that a user of such a script effectively has a context window half the size of an English user's.

### What the builder does

1. Train the vocabulary on a corpus that mirrors the target language mix.
2. Grow the vocabulary so that more merges serve non-Latin scripts; the move from 32K to 128K in one family was made mainly for this.
3. Train with a library that works on raw text without pre-tokenization, so scripts without spaces segment well.
4. Measure fertility per language and report it with the model.

### How to measure it

Take the same 10 meaning-aligned sentences in English, Spanish, Chinese, Korean and Arabic, from one parallel corpus, tokenize each with the candidate vocabulary, and compare the average tokens per character. The ratios are the tax; with sentences that do not match, report them as a spot check only.

## Follow-ups

- **Level 1:** Define fertility in one sentence. Expected: the average number of tokens the tokenizer produces per word, where higher means the model works harder for the same text.
- **Level 2:** How do you measure the tax for a new vocabulary? Expected: tokenize matched sentences in several languages and compare tokens per character or per word.
- **Level 2:** Why does a larger vocabulary help scripts other than English? Expected: more merges can be spent on their byte patterns, so each character or word needs fewer tokens.
